"Nutfah" is a drop; one says "nataf yanti'" meaning it dripped, and "laylatun nutufun" meaning a night of continuous dripping. ﴿Then from a clot﴾: "'alaqah" is congealed blood, and "'alaq" is fresh blood, meaning fresh or congealed. It was said: intensely red. The intended meaning is congealed blood formed from the semen. ﴿Then from a lump﴾: it is a piece of flesh about the size of what a chewer chews, formed from the clot. ﴿Formed﴾ is in the genitive as an attribute of "mudghah," meaning: of clear form, its shape manifest. ﴿And unformed﴾: meaning its form was not clarified and its shape did not appear. Ibn al-A'rabi said: "Formed (mukhallaqah) means its creation has appeared; unformed means it was not shaped." Most said: what has had its creation completed by the breathing of the spirit into it is the "formed," and this is the one born at full term; what fell prematurely was "unformed," meaning not alive, its creation not completed by the spirit. Al-Farra' said: "Mukhallaqah is complete in form, and ghayr mukhallaqah is the miscarriage." From this is the poet's verse:

"Is weeping for an unformed miscarriage, and where is sound judgment, woe to you, and modesty?"

The lam in ﴿that We may make clear to you﴾ is connected to "khalaqna": meaning, We created you in this pattern so that We may make clear to you the perfection of Our power through Our variation of the stages of your creation. ﴿And We settle in the wombs whatever We will﴾: Abu Hatim reported from Abu Zayd from al-Mufaddal from 'Asim that he read "nuqirra" with a fathah, as a conjunction to "nubayyina." The majority read "nuqirru" with a damma, as a new sentence: meaning, and We settle. Al-Zajjaj said: "nuqirru" is only with the damma, because the meaning is not 'We did that so that We might settle in the wombs what We will.' The meaning of the verse is: and We establish in the wombs whatever We will, so it is not a miscarriage." ﴿For a specified term﴾: this is the time of birth. He said "ma nashau" and did not say "man nashau," because it refers to the pregnancy, which is inanimate before the spirit is breathed into it. It was read "liyubayyina," "wa-yuqirru," and "yukhrijukum" with the yā' in the three verbs. Ibn Abi Wathhab read "ma nashau" with a kasra on the nun.

﴿Then We bring you out as infants﴾: meaning, We bring you out from the bellies of your mothers as infants, that is, as children. He used the singular out of intent for the genus, which includes one and many. Al-Zajjaj said: "Tiflan" (infant) is in the sense of "atfalan" (infants), and what indicates this is the mention of the plural in "nukhrijukum." The Arabs often apply the name of the singular to the plural, as in the poet's verse:

"They blame me for her love and rebuke me, but the reproachers are not in authority over me."

Al-Mubarrad said: it is a noun used as a verbal noun, like al-ridā and al-‘adl, so it applies to the singular and the plural. Allah the Glorified said: ﴿or the children who have not yet come to know the private parts of women﴾ [al-Nur: 13]. Ibn Jarir said: it is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz), like His words: ﴿but if they willingly give you some of it, [it is] yours with satisfaction﴾ [al-Nisa’: 4]. But this is far-fetched. The apparent view is that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), by the interpretation mentioned. The word ṭifl (child) is applied to the infant from the time of separation (from the mother) until puberty. ﴿Then that you may reach your maturity (ashudd)﴾. It was said that it is a purpose clause governed by "to bring you out," coordinated with another suitable purpose, as if it were said: "We bring you out so that you may grow up gradually, then so that you may reach maturity." It was also said that thumma (then) is superfluous, and the meaning is "that you may reach." It was also said that it is coordinated with "to make clear." Ashudd is the perfection of intellect, the perfection of strength, and discernment. It was said that it is between thirty and forty years. The discussion of this has been covered fully in (the commentary on) al-An‘am. ﴿And among you is one who is taken in death﴾, meaning before reaching maturity. It has been read as yutawaffā with the active voice, but the majority read yutawaffā in the passive voice. ﴿And among you is one who is returned to the most abject age (ardhal al-‘umr)﴾, that is, its lowest and most degraded point, which is senility and dotage, to the extent that he does not reason. For this reason He, the Glorified, said: ﴿so that he knows nothing after knowing﴾, that is, nothing of things, or nothing of knowledge. The meaning is that he becomes, after having been one who had knowledge of things and understanding of them, one who has neither knowledge nor understanding. A similar statement is His words: ﴿Indeed We created man in the best of stature, then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾ [al-Tin: 4–5], and His words: ﴿And whom We cause to live long, We reverse in creation﴾ [Ya Sin: 68].

﴿And you see the earth lifeless (hamidah)﴾. This is another proof for resurrection, for He, the Glorified, argued from the revival of the earth by sending down water to the revival of the dead. Hamidah means dry, which produces nothing. Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, dead and dry like a fire when it has been extinguished. It was said: effaced (dāri­sah), and humūd means effacement, and from it is the saying of al-A‘sha:

"Qutayla said: 'What ails your body, pale, and I see your garments worn out (bāliyāt) and effaced (humūdan)?'"

It was also said: it is that from which moisture has departed. It was said: perished. The meanings of these sayings are close.

﴿So when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells (ihtazzat wa rabat)﴾. The water here means rain. Ihtazzat means it moved, and ihtizāz means intense movement. It is said: "I shook the thing and it shook (ihtazza)," that is, I moved it and it moved. The meaning is: it moved with vegetation, because vegetation does not come forth from it until it actually displaces part of it from part, so He called it ihtizāz figuratively. Al-Mubarrad said: the meaning is that its vegetation stirred, and the attributive noun was omitted; its stirring is the intensity of its movement, and ihtizāz is more apparent in the vegetation than in the earth. Rabat means it rose up; it was also said it swelled. The meaning is one, and its root is increase. It is said: "rabā al-shay’ yarbū rabwan" when it increased, and from it come ribā (usury) and rabwah (a hill).

Yazid ibn al-Qa‘qa‘ and Khalid ibn Ilyas read (warabaʼat), meaning it rose until it became like a hillock (rābiyah). This is the one who guards a people from an elevated place, called rābiʼ, rābiʼah and rabīʼah. ﴿And it causes to grow (anbatat)﴾, that is, it brings forth ﴿every beautiful pair (zawj bahīj)﴾, that is, every fine kind and pleasing color. Bahjah means beauty.

The clause ﴿That is because Allah, He is the Truth﴾ is a resumptive sentence. After mentioning the dependence of existing things upon Him, the Glorified, and their subjection to His will and power, He said after that these statements, which affirm that He, the Glorified, is the Truth, that He alone revives the dead, and that He is capable of everything. The meaning is that He alone possesses these matters, and they are of His domain; no one else claims to be able to do any of them. Thereby the Glorified indicates that He is the true Truth, the self-sufficient Absolute, and that the existence of every existent is derived from Him. The Truth is the existent that does not change and does not cease. It was said: the Owner of right over His servants. It was said: the Truth in His acts. Al-Zajjaj said: that is in the place of the nominative: that is, the matter is what He described to you, and made clear that Allah is the Truth. He said: it may also be in the accusative.

Then the Glorified informed that ﴿the Hour is coming﴾, that is, in the future. It was said that a verb must be supplied: that is, "and that you may know that the Hour is coming." ﴿There is no doubt about it﴾, that is, no uncertainty or hesitation. The clause ﴿there is no doubt about it﴾ is a second predicate of "the Hour," or in the place of the accusative as a circumstantial state.

Then the Glorified informed about resurrection, saying: ﴿and that Allah will raise up those who are in the graves﴾, and He will recompense them for their deeds: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil, and that this is certainly going to happen.

Sa‘id ibn Mansur, Ahmad, ‘Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), al-Nasa’i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and Ibn Mardawayh reported through various chains from al-Hasan and others, from ‘Imran ibn Husayn, who said: "When the verse ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord. Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing﴾ up to His words ﴿but the punishment of Allah is severe﴾ was revealed, it was revealed to him while he was on a journey. He said: 'Do you know what day that is?' They said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'That is the day when Allah says to Adam: Send forth the group for the Fire.' He said: 'O Lord, what is the group for the Fire?' He said: 'Out of every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine to the Fire, and one to Paradise.' The Muslims began to weep. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Be close to the mark, aim right, and rejoice, for no prophethood has ever been except that before it there was ignorance (jahiliyyah), and the numbers are taken from the ignorance; if they are complete, well, and if not, they are completed from the hypocrites. And your likeness among the nations is only like the spot on the foreleg of a beast, or like the mole on the flank of a camel.' Then he said: 'Indeed I hope that you will be a quarter of the people of Paradise,' and they exclaimed Allahu akbar. Then he said: 'Indeed I hope that you will be a third of the people of Paradise,' and they exclaimed Allahu akbar. Then he said: 'Indeed I hope that you will be half of the people of Paradise,' and they exclaimed Allahu akbar. He said: 'I do not know whether he said two-thirds or not.'"

al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sound, and Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated a similar marfu‘ report from ‘Imran ibn Husayn, and at its end it says: "Act and rejoice, for by Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, you are with two creations that have never been with anything without multiplying it: Ya'juj and Ma'juj, and whoever dies of the children of Adam and of the children of Iblis." So some of what the people were feeling was relieved. He said: "Act and rejoice, for by Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, you are among the people only like the mole on the flank of a camel, or like the spot on the foreleg of a beast."

‘Abd al-Razzaq, ‘Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Anas as a marfu‘ report similar to this. Al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and Ibn Mardawayh also reported from Anas as a marfu‘ report similar to this too. In the two Sahihs and others, from Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said, and he mentioned something similar, and at its end he said: "Of Ya'juj and Ma'juj there are a thousand, and of you there is one. Are you among the nations anything but like a black hair on a white ox, or a white hair on a black ox?"

‘Abd al-Razzaq, ‘Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿it is decreed for him﴾, that he said: "It is decreed for the devil."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ‘Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported a similar statement from Mujahid regarding ﴿that whoever takes him as an ally﴾, that he said: "He follows him."

al-Bukhari, Muslim, the authors of the Sunan, and others reported from Ibn Mas‘ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who is the truthful and the one whose truthfulness is confirmed, told us: "Indeed one of you is gathered in his mother's belly as a drop for forty days, then becomes a clot for a similar period, then becomes a lump of flesh for a similar period. Then Allah sends to him the angel, who breathes into him the soul, and he is commanded with four words: to write his provision, his term, his deeds, and whether he is wretched or happy. By Him other than whom there is no god, indeed one of you acts by the deeds of the people of Paradise until there is between him and it only a cubit, then the Book overtakes him, and he acts by the deeds of the people of the Fire and enters it. And indeed one of you acts by the deeds of the people of the Fire until there is between him and it only a cubit, then the Book overtakes him, and he acts by the deeds of the people of Paradise and enters it."

The reports on this subject are very numerous.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported, and graded it sound, from Ibn ‘Abbas regarding His words ﴿formed and unformed﴾, that he said: "The formed (mukhallaqah) is that which was alive, and the unformed (ghayr mukhallaqah) is that which was a miscarriage." Similar was reported from a group of the Successors.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ‘Abbas regarding His words ﴿of every beautiful pair﴾, that he said: "Beautiful."

‘Abd Allah ibn Ahmad, in the Zawa'id of al-Zuhd, reported from Mu‘adh ibn Jabal, who said: "Whoever knows that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is the Truth, and that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it, and that Allah will raise up those in the graves, will enter Paradise."

**Fath al-Qadir of al-Shawkani, commentary on surah 22, verses 8–16 (part 1 of 2)**

.

His words, ﴿And among mankind is one who disputes about God﴾, mean: about the affairs of God, like the one who says that the angels are the daughters of God, that the Messiah is the son of God, and that ʿUzayr is the son of God. It has been said that it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and it has been said that it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl. It has also been said that it is general to everyone who sets himself up to lead people astray and mislead them. In any case, what counts is the general meaning of the wording, even if the occasion of revelation is specific. The meaning of the wording is: among mankind is a group who disputes about God, so this includes everyone who disputes about the essence of God, or His attributes, or His clear laws. ﴿Without knowledge﴾ is in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), meaning: while being without knowledge. It has been said that by knowledge is meant necessary knowledge (ʿilm ḍarūrī), and by guidance is meant acquired, reasoned knowledge (ʿilm naẓarī istidlālī). The better view is to take knowledge in its general sense and to take guidance in its linguistic meaning, which is direction. By the illuminating Book is meant the Qur'an. "Illuminating" (munīr) means shining, clear in proof, and evident in demonstration. Although it falls under His words ﴿without knowledge﴾, singling it out for mention is like singling out Gabriel for mention after mentioning the angels, because it is the complete example that surpasses other examples of knowledge. As for the one who takes knowledge to mean necessary knowledge and guidance to mean reasoned knowledge, he takes the Book here to mean the transmitted evidence (al-dalīl al-samʿī). Then the verse includes the negation of rational evidence, whether necessary or reasoned, and also includes the negation of transmitted evidence in all its forms. What we have mentioned is the better view. It has been said that by this disputant in this verse is meant the disputant in the first verse, namely His words ﴿And among mankind is one who disputes about God without knowledge, and follows every rebellious devil﴾ [al-Hajj: 3]. Many exegetes have said this. The repetition is for emphasis in censure, as when you say to a man whom you are rebuking and reproaching: "You did this, you did this?" It is also possible that the repetition is because He described him in each verse with something additional to what He described him with in the other verse. It is as if He said: "And among mankind is one who disputes about God and follows every rebellious devil without knowledge, ﴿and without guidance or an illuminating Book﴾, in order to lead astray from the way of God." End of quotation. It has also been said that the first verse concerns those who imitate (muqallidūn) in the form of the active participle, and the second concerns those who are imitated in the form of the passive participle. The second is general to every act of misleading and disputing. The accusative of ﴿turning his side﴾ is a ḥāl from the subject of "disputes." ʿIṭf means the side, and the two ʿiṭfs of a man are his two sides, right and left. There are two views on its interpretation. The first is that it means one who twists his neck out of insolence and arrogance. al-Zajjaj mentioned this meaning and said: "This is how the arrogant person is described." The meaning is: among mankind is one who disputes about God arrogantly. al-Mubarrad said: "ʿIṭf is the part of the neck that is bent." The second view is that His words ﴿turning his side﴾ mean turning away: that is, turning away from the remembrance. This was said by al-Farra', al-Mufaḍḍal, and others, as in His words: ﴿He turned away arrogantly as if he had not heard it﴾ [Luqman: 7], His words ﴿They turned their heads﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 5], and His words ﴿He turned away and withdrew with his side﴾ [al-Isra': 83]. The lam in ﴿in order to lead astray from the way of God﴾ is connected to "disputes": that is, his aim is to lead astray from the way, even if he does not admit it. It was read as "li-yaḍilla" (with a fatḥa on the yāʾ), in which case the lam is the lam of consequence (lam al-ʿāqibah), as if He made his going astray the end of his disputing. The clause ﴿For him in this world is disgrace﴾ is a new (resumed) sentence explaining what results for him from his disputing, namely the punishment. Khizy means humiliation. This is by the punishment he receives in this world, which is the hastened torment and evil mention on people's tongues. It has been said that the worldly disgrace is death, as happened on the day of Badr. ﴿And We will make him taste on the Day of Resurrection the punishment of the burning﴾, that is, the punishment of the burning Fire. The demonstrative in His words "that" refers to what preceded of worldly and otherworldly punishment (p-956). It is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿for what your hands have sent forth﴾. The bāʾ is causal: that is, that punishment which descends upon you is because of what your hands have sent forth of disbelief and sins. He expressed the whole body by "hands" because the commission of sins is generally done with them. The position of "that" (anna) and what follows it in His words ﴿and that God is not unjust to the servants﴾ is nominative, as its predicate for an omitted subject: that is, the matter is that He, glorified is He, does not punish His servants without sin. The discussion of this verse has already passed at the end of Al ʿImran, so we will not repeat it.

﴿And among mankind is one who worships God on a harf﴾. This is an explanation of the conduct of the people of dissension (ahl al-shiqaq). al-Wahidi said: Most exegetes said: the harf is doubt. Its origin is from the edge (ḥarf) of a thing, like the edge of a mountain or a wall, for one standing on it is not steady. The one who worships God on a harf is restless in his religion, without firmness and tranquility, like one who is on the edge of a mountain or the like, who shakes violently and whose standing weakens. So the one who doubts his religion is said to worship God on a harf, because he is not certain of His promise and threat, unlike the believer, who worships Him with certainty and insight, so he is not on a harf. It has also been said: the harf is a condition, meaning: among mankind is one who worships God on a condition, and the condition is His words ﴿If good befalls him, he is content with it﴾, that is, worldly good of prosperity, well-being, abundance, and much wealth. The meaning of "is content with it" is that he remains firm in his religion and persists in his worship, or that his heart is at rest with that good which has befallen him. ﴿But if an ordeal befalls him﴾, that is, something by which he is tested, of a disliked kind that afflicts him in his family, his property, or himself, ﴿he turns over on his face﴾, that is, he apostatizes and returns to the state of disbelief he had been in. Then He described his condition after his turning over on his face, saying: ﴿He has lost this world and the Hereafter﴾, that is, he has gone and lost both. So he has no share in this world of spoils and good repute, nor in the Hereafter of reward and what God has prepared for His righteous servants. Mujahid, Humayd ibn Qays, al-Aʿraj, al-Zuhri, and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "khasira" in the form of the active participle, "khasiran al-dunya wa'l-akhirah," in the accusative as a ḥāl. It was also read in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject. The demonstrative in His words "that" refers to the loss of this world and the Hereafter, and it is the subject, with its predicate ﴿that is the manifest loss﴾, that is, the clear, evident loss to which there is no equal. ﴿He calls upon, besides God, that which neither harms him nor benefits him﴾, that is, this one who turned over on his face and returned to disbelief calls upon, besides God, meaning he worships, going beyond the worship of God to the worship of idols, that which does not harm him if he abandons its worship, nor benefit him if he worships it, because that object of worship is inanimate and has no power over harm or benefit. The demonstrative in His words "that" refers to the calling, which is understood from the verb "he calls," and the demonstrative is a subject whose predicate is ﴿That is the far-off error﴾, that is, far from truth and right guidance. It is a metaphor taken from the error of one who goes by other than the road and, by his error, becomes far from it. al-Farra' said: "Baʿid" means long.

﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾. "Yadʿu" here means "yaqūlu" (says). The clause confirms what precedes it, namely that this calling is far-off error. Idols have no benefit in them in any way at all; rather, they are pure harm to the one who worships them, because he has entered the Fire because of worshipping them. The use of the comparative form, despite the total absence of benefit, is for emphasis in disparaging the condition of that caller, or it is of the kind of His words ﴿Indeed, we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Saba': 24]. The lam is the one preparing for the oath (al-lām al-muwaṭṭiʾah lil-qasam), and "man" is a relative pronoun or a qualifying noun. "Darruhu" is the subject, whose predicate is "aqrabu," and the clause is the relative clause. The clause ﴿Surely the worst patron and the worst companion﴾ is the answer to the oath. The meaning is: that disbeliever will say that on the Day of Resurrection to the one he worshipped, whose harm is nearer than his benefit: "Worst is the patron you are, and worst is the companion." al-Mawla is the helper, and al-ʿashir is the companion. Like what is in this verse is the saying of ʿAntarah:

They call on ʿAntarah while the spears are like the ropes of a well
in the chest of the dark-coloured horse.

al-Zajjaj said: It is possible that "yadʿu" is in the position of a ḥāl, and in it there is an omitted pronoun, meaning: that is the far-off error, he calls it. In this case one stops at "yadʿu," and His words ﴿for him whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾ form a new sentence, nominative by the inception, whose predicate is "la-bi'sa al-mawla" (surely worst is the patron). He said: This is because the lam is for the oath and emphasis, so he placed it at the beginning of the sentence.

al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' said: It is possible that "yadʿu" is repeated upon what precedes it, as an intensification of this action, which is calling: that is, he calls upon what neither harms him nor benefits him, he calls. Like "I struck Zayd, I struck." al-Farra', al-Kisa'i, and al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of the sentence is an oath, and the lam is placed before its proper position, and the estimate is: "He calls upon whoever surely whose harm is nearer than his benefit." So "man" is in the accusative position governed by "yadʿu," the lam is the answer to the oath, "darruhu" is the subject, and "aqrabu" is its predicate. Among the rearrangements of the lam by fronting and postponing is the poet's saying:

My uncle, you surely are, and whoever Jarir is his uncle,
will attain glory and honour the maternal uncles.

That is: "Surely you are my uncle." al-Nahhas said: ʿAli ibn Sulayman related to us from Muhammad ibn Yazid, who said: "There is an omission in the sentence, and the meaning is: he calls upon for whoever's harm is nearer than his benefit a god." al-Nahhas said: I think this statement is a mistake from Muhammad ibn Yazid, and perhaps its basis is that what comes before this lam does not govern what comes after it. al-Farra' also and al-Qaffal said: the lam is a ṣilah, that is, superfluous, and the meaning is: he calls upon whoever's harm is nearer than his benefit, that is, he worships him. Likewise in the reading of ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, with the lam omitted. On this view the lam in "la-bi'sa al-mawla" and in "la-bi'sa al-ʿashir" is the one preparing for the oath.

﴿Indeed, God will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. When He finished mentioning the condition of the polytheists, and of the one who worships God on a harf, He mentioned the condition of the believers in the Hereafter, and informed that He will admit them into these gardens which have this description. The discussion of rivers flowing beneath them has already passed, and it is clear. If by "gardens" is meant the land, then a genitive noun must be estimated: that is, beneath its trees. ﴿Indeed, God does what He wills﴾. This sentence is a reason for what precedes it: that is, He does what He wills of acts, ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ [al-Anbiya': 23], so He rewards whom He wills and punishes whom He wills.

﴿Whoever thinks that God will not help him in this world and the Hereafter﴾. al-Nahhas said: Among the best things said about this verse is that the meaning is: whoever thinks that God will not help Muhammad, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, and that it is possible for him to cut off the help that he has been given. ﴿Let him stretch a rope to the sky﴾, that is, let him seek a means by which he reaches the sky, then let him cut, that is, then let him cut off the help if it is possible for him. ﴿Then let him look: will his scheme remove what enrages him?﴾ His scheme and stratagem is what enrages him of the help of the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace. It has been said that the meaning is: whoever thinks that God will not help Muhammad until He makes him prevail over all religion, then let him die of rage. Then he explained it by His words ﴿Let him stretch a rope to the sky﴾, that is, let him tie a rope to the ceiling of his house. ﴿Then let him cut﴾, that is, then let him pull the rope until it breaks, so that he dies strangled. The meaning is: let him choke with rage until he dies, for God is his helper and the one who makes him prevail, and his rage will not benefit him. The meaning of "then let him look: will his scheme remove what enrages him?" is: his action and stratagem, what enrages, that is, his rage; "ma" is a verbal noun (maṣdariyyah). It has been said that the pronoun in "yanṣuruhu" refers to "man," and the meaning is: whoever thinks that God does not provide for him, let him kill himself, and Abu ʿUbaydah said this. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the religion: that is, whoever thinks that God will not help His religion. The Kufans read "thumma li-yaqṭaʿ" with the lam of the imperative sukūn. al-Nahhas said: This reading is far from the Arabic language.

(p-957)

Thus We have sent it down as clear signs, meaning: in the same wondrous manner of sending down, We have sent it down as clear signs whose indications are evident in what they signify. ﴿And that Allah guides whom He wills﴾, meaning whose guidance He wills, either initially or by increasing it for one who was already guided before.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from Qatada, regarding His words ﴿turning his side﴾, that he said: "Twisting his neck."

Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Jurayj that it means "the one who turns away."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported regarding His words ﴿turning his side﴾ that he said: "It was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Ḥarith."

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse that he said: "He is a man from the Banu ʿAbd al-Dar."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿And among the people is one who worships Allah on an edge﴾ that he said: "A man would come to Madina, and if his wife bore a son and his mares foaled, he would say, 'This is a good religion.' But if his wife did not bear and his mares did not foal, he would say, 'This is a bad religion.'"

Ibn Abi Ḥatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him, with a sound chain, that he said: "Some Bedouins would come to the Prophet (ﷺ) and embrace Islam. When they returned to their lands, if they found a year of rain, a year of fertility and a year of good births, they would say, 'Indeed, this religion of ours is good, so hold fast to it.' But if they found a year of drought, a year of bad births and a year of famine, they would say, 'There is nothing good in this religion of ours.' So Allah revealed: ﴿And among the people is one who worships Allah on an edge﴾."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Ḥatim and Ibn Mardawayh also reported from him something similar, and in its chain is al-ʿAwfi.

Ibn Mardawayh also reported through the same route from Abu Saʿid that he said: "A man from the Jews embraced Islam, then he lost his sight, his wealth and his child, so he considered Islam an ill omen. He came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said, 'Release me, release me!' He (ﷺ) said, 'Islam cannot be relinquished.' The man said, 'I have gained nothing good from this religion of mine: I lost my sight, my wealth, and my child died.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said, 'O Jew, Islam refines men as fire refines the dross of iron, gold and silver.' So there was revealed: ﴿And among the people is one who worships Allah on an edge﴾."

al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥatim, al-Ḥakim (who declared it sound) and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿Whoever thinks that Allah will not help him﴾ that he said: "Whoever thinks that Allah will not help Muhammad in this world and the Hereafter." ﴿Let him extend a rope﴾: "Let him tie it." ﴿to the sky﴾: "to the ceiling of his house." ﴿then let him cut it off﴾: "then let him strangle himself with it until he dies."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from him that he said: ﴿Whoever thinks that Allah will not help him﴾ means: "that Allah will not provide for him." ﴿Let him extend a rope to the sky﴾: "let him take a rope and tie it to the ceiling of his house, then let him strangle himself with it." ﴿Then let him see whether his scheme removes that which enrages him﴾: "let him see whether that benefits him, or brings him provision."

﴿And among mankind is one who worships God on a harf﴾. This is an explanation of the conduct of the people of dissension (ahl al-shiqaq). al-Wahidi said: Most exegetes said: the harf is doubt. Then He described his condition after his turning over on his face, saying: ﴿He has lost this world and the Hereafter﴾, that is, he has gone and lost both. So he has no share in this world of spoils and good repute, nor in the Hereafter of reward and what God has prepared for His righteous servants. It is a metaphor taken from the error of one who goes by other than the road and, by his error, becomes far from it. al-Farra' said: "Baʿid" means long.

﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾. "Yadʿu" here means "yaqūlu" (says). The clause confirms what precedes it, namely that this calling is far-off error. Idols have no benefit in them in any way at all; rather, they are pure harm to the one who worships them, because he has entered the Fire because of worshipping them. They call on ʿAntarah while the spears are like the ropes of a well
in the chest of the dark-coloured horse.

al-Zajjaj said: It is possible that "yadʿu" is in the position of a ḥāl, and in it there is an omitted pronoun, meaning: that is the far-off error, he calls it. He said: This is because the lam is for the oath and emphasis, so he placed it at the beginning of the sentence.

Like "I struck Zayd, I struck." al-Farra', al-Kisa'i, and al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of the sentence is an oath, and the lam is placed before its proper position, and the estimate is: "He calls upon whoever surely whose harm is nearer than his benefit." My uncle, you surely are, and whoever Jarir is his uncle,
will attain glory and honour the maternal uncles.

That is: "Surely you are my uncle." al-Nahhas said: ʿAli ibn Sulayman related to us from Muhammad ibn Yazid, who said: "There is an omission in the sentence, and the meaning is: he calls upon for whoever's harm is nearer than his benefit a god." al-Nahhas said: I think this statement is a mistake from Muhammad ibn Yazid, and perhaps its basis is that what comes before this lam does not govern what comes after it. al-Farra' also and al-Qaffal said: the lam is a ṣilah, that is, superfluous, and the meaning is: he calls upon whoever's harm is nearer than his benefit, that is, he worships him. The discussion of rivers flowing beneath them has already passed, and it is clear. It has been said that the meaning is: whoever thinks that God will not help Muhammad until He makes him prevail over all religion, then let him die of rage. It has been said that the pronoun in "yanṣuruhu" refers to "man," and the meaning is: whoever thinks that God does not provide for him, let him kill himself, and Abu ʿUbaydah said this. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the religion: that is, whoever thinks that God will not help His religion. The Kufans read "thumma li-yaqṭaʿ" with the lam of the imperative sukūn. al-Nahhas said: This reading is far from the Arabic language.

(p-957)

Thus We have sent it down as clear signs, meaning: in the same wondrous manner of sending down, We have sent it down as clear signs whose indications are evident in what they signify. ﴿And that Allah guides whom He wills﴾, meaning whose guidance He wills, either initially or by increasing it for one who was already guided before.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from Qatada, regarding His words ﴿turning his side﴾, that he said: "Twisting his neck."

Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Jurayj that it means "the one who turns away."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported regarding His words ﴿turning his side﴾ that he said: "It was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Ḥarith."

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse that he said: "He is a man from the Banu ʿAbd al-Dar."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿And among the people is one who worships Allah on an edge﴾ that he said: "A man would come to Madina, and if his wife bore a son and his mares foaled, he would say, 'This is a good religion.' But if his wife did not bear and his mares did not foal, he would say, 'This is a bad religion.'"

Ibn Abi Ḥatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him, with a sound chain, that he said: "Some Bedouins would come to the Prophet (ﷺ) and embrace Islam. When they returned to their lands, if they found a year of rain, a year of fertility and a year of good births, they would say, 'Indeed, this religion of ours is good, so hold fast to it.' But if they found a year of drought, a year of bad births and a year of famine, they would say, 'There is nothing good in this religion of ours.' So Allah revealed: ﴿And among the people is one who worships Allah on an edge﴾."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Ḥatim and Ibn Mardawayh also reported from him something similar, and in its chain is al-ʿAwfi.

Ibn Mardawayh also reported through the same route from Abu Saʿid that he said: "A man from the Jews embraced Islam, then he lost his sight, his wealth and his child, so he considered Islam an ill omen. He came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said, 'Release me, release me!' He (ﷺ) said, 'Islam cannot be relinquished.' The man said, 'I have gained nothing good from this religion of mine: I lost my sight, my wealth, and my child died.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said, 'O Jew, Islam refines men as fire refines the dross of iron, gold and silver.' So there was revealed: ﴿And among the people is one who worships Allah on an edge﴾."

al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥatim, al-Ḥakim (who declared it sound) and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿Whoever thinks that Allah will not help him﴾ that he said: "Whoever thinks that Allah will not help Muhammad in this world and the Hereafter." ﴿Let him extend a rope﴾: "Let him tie it." ﴿to the sky﴾: "to the ceiling of his house." ﴿then let him cut it off﴾: "then let him strangle himself with it until he dies."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from him that he said: ﴿Whoever thinks that Allah will not help him﴾ means: "that Allah will not provide for him." ﴿Let him extend a rope to the sky﴾: "let him take a rope and tie it to the ceiling of his house, then let him strangle himself with it." ﴿Then let him see whether his scheme removes that which enrages him﴾: "let him see whether that benefits him, or brings him provision."

His words, ﴿And among mankind is one who disputes about God﴾, mean: about the affairs of God, like the one who says that the angels are the daughters of God, that the Messiah is the son of God, and that ʿUzayr is the son of God. It has also been said that it is general to everyone who sets himself up to lead people astray and mislead them. In any case, what counts is the general meaning of the wording, even if the occasion of revelation is specific. The meaning of the wording is: among mankind is a group who disputes about God, so this includes everyone who disputes about the essence of God, or His attributes, or His clear laws. ﴿Without knowledge﴾ is in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), meaning: while being without knowledge. It has been said that by knowledge is meant necessary knowledge (ʿilm ḍarūrī), and by guidance is meant acquired, reasoned knowledge (ʿilm naẓarī istidlālī). The better view is to take knowledge in its general sense and to take guidance in its linguistic meaning, which is direction. By the illuminating Book is meant the Qur'an. "Illuminating" (munīr) means shining, clear in proof, and evident in demonstration. Although it falls under His words ﴿without knowledge﴾, singling it out for mention is like singling out Gabriel for mention after mentioning the angels, because it is the complete example that surpasses other examples of knowledge. As for the one who takes knowledge to mean necessary knowledge and guidance to mean reasoned knowledge, he takes the Book here to mean the transmitted evidence (al-dalīl al-samʿī). Then the verse includes the negation of rational evidence, whether necessary or reasoned, and also includes the negation of transmitted evidence in all its forms. What we have mentioned is the better view. It has been said that by this disputant in this verse is meant the disputant in the first verse, namely His words ﴿And among mankind is one who disputes about God without knowledge, and follows every rebellious devil﴾ [al-Hajj: 3]. Many exegetes have said this. The repetition is for emphasis in censure, as when you say to a man whom you are rebuking and reproaching: "You did this, you did this?" It is also possible that the repetition is because He described him in each verse with something additional to what He described him with in the other verse. It is as if He said: "And among mankind is one who disputes about God and follows every rebellious devil without knowledge, ﴿and without guidance or an illuminating Book﴾, in order to lead astray from the way of God." End of quotation. It has also been said that the first verse concerns those who imitate (muqallidūn) in the form of the active participle, and the second concerns those who are imitated in the form of the passive participle. The second is general to every act of misleading and disputing. The accusative of ﴿turning his side﴾ is a ḥāl from the subject of "disputes." ʿIṭf means the side, and the two ʿiṭfs of a man are his two sides, right and left. There are two views on its interpretation. The first is that it means one who twists his neck out of insolence and arrogance. al-Zajjaj mentioned this meaning and said: "This is how the arrogant person is described." The meaning is: among mankind is one who disputes about God arrogantly. al-Mubarrad said: "ʿIṭf is the part of the neck that is bent." The second view is that His words ﴿turning his side﴾ mean turning away: that is, turning away from the remembrance. This was said by al-Farra', al-Mufaḍḍal, and others, as in His words: ﴿He turned away arrogantly as if he had not heard it﴾ [Luqman: 7], His words ﴿They turned their heads﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 5], and His words ﴿He turned away and withdrew with his side﴾ [al-Isra': 83]. The lam in ﴿in order to lead astray from the way of God﴾ is connected to "disputes": that is, his aim is to lead astray from the way, even if he does not admit it. It was read as "li-yaḍilla" (with a fatḥa on the yāʾ), in which case the lam is the lam of consequence (lam al-ʿāqibah), as if He made his going astray the end of his disputing. The clause ﴿For him in this world is disgrace﴾ is a new (resumed) sentence explaining what results for him from his disputing, namely the punishment. Khizy means humiliation. This is by the punishment he receives in this world, which is the hastened torment and evil mention on people's tongues. It has been said that the worldly disgrace is death, as happened on the day of Badr. ﴿And We will make him taste on the Day of Resurrection the punishment of the burning﴾, that is, the punishment of the burning Fire. The demonstrative in His words "that" refers to what preceded of worldly and otherworldly punishment (p-956). It is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿for what your hands have sent forth﴾. The bāʾ is causal: that is, that punishment which descends upon you is because of what your hands have sent forth of disbelief and sins. He expressed the whole body by "hands" because the commission of sins is generally done with them. The position of "that" (anna) and what follows it in His words ﴿and that God is not unjust to the servants﴾ is nominative, as its predicate for an omitted subject: that is, the matter is that He, glorified is He, does not punish His servants without sin. The discussion of this verse has already passed at the end of Al ʿImran, so we will not repeat it.

﴿And among mankind is one who worships God on a harf﴾. This is an explanation of the conduct of the people of dissension (ahl al-shiqaq). al-Wahidi said: Most exegetes said: the harf is doubt. Its origin is from the edge (ḥarf) of a thing, like the edge of a mountain or a wall, for one standing on it is not steady. The one who worships God on a harf is restless in his religion, without firmness and tranquility, like one who is on the edge of a mountain or the like, who shakes violently and whose standing weakens. So the one who doubts his religion is said to worship God on a harf, because he is not certain of His promise and threat, unlike the believer, who worships Him with certainty and insight, so he is not on a harf. It has also been said: the harf is a condition, meaning: among mankind is one who worships God on a condition, and the condition is His words ﴿If good befalls him, he is content with it﴾, that is, worldly good of prosperity, well-being, abundance, and much wealth. The meaning of "is content with it" is that he remains firm in his religion and persists in his worship, or that his heart is at rest with that good which has befallen him. ﴿But if an ordeal befalls him﴾, that is, something by which he is tested, of a disliked kind that afflicts him in his family, his property, or himself, ﴿he turns over on his face﴾, that is, he apostatizes and returns to the state of disbelief he had been in. Then He described his condition after his turning over on his face, saying: ﴿He has lost this world and the Hereafter﴾, that is, he has gone and lost both. So he has no share in this world of spoils and good repute, nor in the Hereafter of reward and what God has prepared for His righteous servants. Mujahid, Humayd ibn Qays, al-Aʿraj, al-Zuhri, and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "khasira" in the form of the active participle, "khasiran al-dunya wa'l-akhirah," in the accusative as a ḥāl. It was also read in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject. The demonstrative in His words "that" refers to the loss of this world and the Hereafter, and it is the subject, with its predicate ﴿that is the manifest loss﴾, that is, the clear, evident loss to which there is no equal. ﴿He calls upon, besides God, that which neither harms him nor benefits him﴾, that is, this one who turned over on his face and returned to disbelief calls upon, besides God, meaning he worships, going beyond the worship of God to the worship of idols, that which does not harm him if he abandons its worship, nor benefit him if he worships it, because that object of worship is inanimate and has no power over harm or benefit. The demonstrative in His words "that" refers to the calling, which is understood from the verb "he calls," and the demonstrative is a subject whose predicate is ﴿That is the far-off error﴾, that is, far from truth and right guidance. It is a metaphor taken from the error of one who goes by other than the road and, by his error, becomes far from it. al-Farra' said: "Baʿid" means long.

﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾. "Yadʿu" here means "yaqūlu" (says). The clause confirms what precedes it, namely that this calling is far-off error. Idols have no benefit in them in any way at all; rather, they are pure harm to the one who worships them, because he has entered the Fire because of worshipping them. The use of the comparative form, despite the total absence of benefit, is for emphasis in disparaging the condition of that caller, or it is of the kind of His words ﴿Indeed, we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Saba': 24]. The lam is the one preparing for the oath (al-lām al-muwaṭṭiʾah lil-qasam), and "man" is a relative pronoun or a qualifying noun. "Darruhu" is the subject, whose predicate is "aqrabu," and the clause is the relative clause. The clause ﴿Surely the worst patron and the worst companion﴾ is the answer to the oath. The meaning is: that disbeliever will say that on the Day of Resurrection to the one he worshipped, whose harm is nearer than his benefit: "Worst is the patron you are, and worst is the companion." al-Mawla is the helper, and al-ʿashir is the companion. Like what is in this verse is the saying of ʿAntarah:

They call on ʿAntarah while the spears are like the ropes of a well
in the chest of the dark-coloured horse.

al-Zajjaj said: It is possible that "yadʿu" is in the position of a ḥāl, and in it there is an omitted pronoun, meaning: that is the far-off error, he calls it. In this case one stops at "yadʿu," and His words ﴿for him whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾ form a new sentence, nominative by the inception, whose predicate is "la-bi'sa al-mawla" (surely worst is the patron). He said: This is because the lam is for the oath and emphasis, so he placed it at the beginning of the sentence.

al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' said: It is possible that "yadʿu" is repeated upon what precedes it, as an intensification of this action, which is calling: that is, he calls upon what neither harms him nor benefits him, he calls. Like "I struck Zayd, I struck." al-Farra', al-Kisa'i, and al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of the sentence is an oath, and the lam is placed before its proper position, and the estimate is: "He calls upon whoever surely whose harm is nearer than his benefit." So "man" is in the accusative position governed by "yadʿu," the lam is the answer to the oath, "darruhu" is the subject, and "aqrabu" is its predicate. Among the rearrangements of the lam by fronting and postponing is the poet's saying:

My uncle, you surely are, and whoever Jarir is his uncle,
will attain glory and honour the maternal uncles.

That is: "Surely you are my uncle." al-Nahhas said: ʿAli ibn Sulayman related to us from Muhammad ibn Yazid, who said: "There is an omission in the sentence, and the meaning is: he calls upon for whoever's harm is nearer than his benefit a god." al-Nahhas said: I think this statement is a mistake from Muhammad ibn Yazid, and perhaps its basis is that what comes before this lam does not govern what comes after it. al-Farra' also and al-Qaffal said: the lam is a ṣilah, that is, superfluous, and the meaning is: he calls upon whoever's harm is nearer than his benefit, that is, he worships him. Likewise in the reading of ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, with the lam omitted. On this view the lam in "la-bi'sa al-mawla" and in "la-bi'sa al-ʿashir" is the one preparing for the oath.

﴿Indeed, God will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. When He finished mentioning the condition of the polytheists, and of the one who worships God on a harf, He mentioned the condition of the believers in the Hereafter, and informed that He will admit them into these gardens which have this description. The discussion of rivers flowing beneath them has already passed, and it is clear. If by "gardens" is meant the land, then a genitive noun must be estimated: that is, beneath its trees. ﴿Indeed, God does what He wills﴾. This sentence is a reason for what precedes it: that is, He does what He wills of acts, ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ [al-Anbiya': 23], so He rewards whom He wills and punishes whom He wills.

in the chest of the dark-coloured horse.

will attain glory and honour the maternal uncles.

Thus We have sent it down as clear signs, meaning: in the same wondrous manner of sending down, We have sent it down as clear signs whose indications are evident in what they signify. ﴿And that Allah guides whom He wills﴾, meaning whose guidance He wills, either initially or by increasing it for one who was already guided before.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse that he said: "He is a man from the Banu ʿAbd al-Dar."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿And among the people is one who worships Allah on an edge﴾ that he said: "A man would come to Madina, and if his wife bore a son and his mares foaled, he would say, 'This is a good religion.' But if his wife did not bear and his mares did not foal, he would say, 'This is a bad religion.'"

Ibn Abi Ḥatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him, with a sound chain, that he said: "Some Bedouins would come to the Prophet (ﷺ) and embrace Islam. When they returned to their lands, if they found a year of rain, a year of fertility and a year of good births, they would say, 'Indeed, this religion of ours is good, so hold fast to it.' But if they found a year of drought, a year of bad births and a year of famine, they would say, 'There is nothing good in this religion of ours.' So Allah revealed: ﴿And among the people is one who worships Allah on an edge﴾."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Ḥatim and Ibn Mardawayh also reported from him something similar, and in its chain is al-ʿAwfi.

Ibn Mardawayh also reported through the same route from Abu Saʿid that he said: "A man from the Jews embraced Islam, then he lost his sight, his wealth and his child, so he considered Islam an ill omen. He came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said, 'Release me, release me!' He (ﷺ) said, 'Islam cannot be relinquished.' The man said, 'I have gained nothing good from this religion of mine: I lost my sight, my wealth, and my child died.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said, 'O Jew, Islam refines men as fire refines the dross of iron, gold and silver.' So there was revealed: ﴿And among the people is one who worships Allah on an edge﴾."

al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥatim, al-Ḥakim (who declared it sound) and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿Whoever thinks that Allah will not help him﴾ that he said: "Whoever thinks that Allah will not help Muhammad in this world and the Hereafter." ﴿Let him extend a rope﴾: "Let him tie it." ﴿to the sky﴾: "to the ceiling of his house." ﴿then let him cut it off﴾: "then let him strangle himself with it until he dies."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from him that he said: ﴿Whoever thinks that Allah will not help him﴾ means: "that Allah will not provide for him." ﴿Let him extend a rope to the sky﴾: "let him take a rope and tie it to the ceiling of his house, then let him strangle himself with it." ﴿Then let him see whether his scheme removes that which enrages him﴾: "let him see whether that benefits him, or brings him provision."

His words, ﴿And among mankind is one who disputes about God﴾, mean: about the affairs of God, like the one who says that the angels are the daughters of God, that the Messiah is the son of God, and that ʿUzayr is the son of God. It has been said that it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and it has been said that it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl. It has also been said that it is general to everyone who sets himself up to lead people astray and mislead them. In any case, what counts is the general meaning of the wording, even if the occasion of revelation is specific. The meaning of the wording is: among mankind is a group who disputes about God, so this includes everyone who disputes about the essence of God, or His attributes, or His clear laws. ﴿Without knowledge﴾ is in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), meaning: while being without knowledge. It has been said that by knowledge is meant necessary knowledge (ʿilm ḍarūrī), and by guidance is meant acquired, reasoned knowledge (ʿilm naẓarī istidlālī). The better view is to take knowledge in its general sense and to take guidance in its linguistic meaning, which is direction. By the illuminating Book is meant the Qur'an. "Illuminating" (munīr) means shining, clear in proof, and evident in demonstration. Although it falls under His words ﴿without knowledge﴾, singling it out for mention is like singling out Gabriel for mention after mentioning the angels, because it is the complete example that surpasses other examples of knowledge. As for the one who takes knowledge to mean necessary knowledge and guidance to mean reasoned knowledge, he takes the Book here to mean the transmitted evidence (al-dalīl al-samʿī). Then the verse includes the negation of rational evidence, whether necessary or reasoned, and also includes the negation of transmitted evidence in all its forms. What we have mentioned is the better view. It has been said that by this disputant in this verse is meant the disputant in the first verse, namely His words ﴿And among mankind is one who disputes about God without knowledge, and follows every rebellious devil﴾ [al-Hajj: 3]. It is also possible that the repetition is because He described him in each verse with something additional to what He described him with in the other verse. It is as if He said: "And among mankind is one who disputes about God and follows every rebellious devil without knowledge, ﴿and without guidance or an illuminating Book﴾, in order to lead astray from the way of God." End of quotation. It has also been said that the first verse concerns those who imitate (muqallidūn) in the form of the active participle, and the second concerns those who are imitated in the form of the passive participle. The accusative of ﴿turning his side﴾ is a ḥāl from the subject of "disputes." ʿIṭf means the side, and the two ʿiṭfs of a man are his two sides, right and left. There are two views on its interpretation. The first is that it means one who twists his neck out of insolence and arrogance. al-Zajjaj mentioned this meaning and said: "This is how the arrogant person is described." The meaning is: among mankind is one who disputes about God arrogantly. al-Mubarrad said: "ʿIṭf is the part of the neck that is bent." The second view is that His words ﴿turning his side﴾ mean turning away: that is, turning away from the remembrance. This was said by al-Farra', al-Mufaḍḍal, and others, as in His words: ﴿He turned away arrogantly as if he had not heard it﴾ [Luqman: 7], His words ﴿They turned their heads﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 5], and His words ﴿He turned away and withdrew with his side﴾ [al-Isra': 83]. The lam in ﴿in order to lead astray from the way of God﴾ is connected to "disputes": that is, his aim is to lead astray from the way, even if he does not admit it. The clause ﴿For him in this world is disgrace﴾ is a new (resumed) sentence explaining what results for him from his disputing, namely the punishment. Khizy means humiliation. This is by the punishment he receives in this world, which is the hastened torment and evil mention on people's tongues. It has been said that the worldly disgrace is death, as happened on the day of Badr. ﴿And We will make him taste on the Day of Resurrection the punishment of the burning﴾, that is, the punishment of the burning Fire. His words, ﴿And among mankind is one who disputes about God﴾, mean: about the affairs of God, like the one who says that the angels are the daughters of God, that the Messiah is the son of God, and that ʿUzayr is the son of God. The better view is to take knowledge in its general sense and to take guidance in its linguistic meaning, which is direction. By the illuminating Book is meant the Qur'an. "Illuminating" (munīr) means shining, clear in proof, and evident in demonstration. Although it falls under His words ﴿without knowledge﴾, singling it out for mention is like singling out Gabriel for mention after mentioning the angels, because it is the complete example that surpasses other examples of knowledge. As for the one who takes knowledge to mean necessary knowledge and guidance to mean reasoned knowledge, he takes the Book here to mean the transmitted evidence (al-dalīl al-samʿī). Then the verse includes the negation of rational evidence, whether necessary or reasoned, and also includes the negation of transmitted evidence in all its forms. What we have mentioned is the better view. It has been said that by this disputant in this verse is meant the disputant in the first verse, namely His words ﴿And among mankind is one who disputes about God without knowledge, and follows every rebellious devil﴾ [al-Hajj: 3]. Many exegetes have said this. The repetition is for emphasis in censure, as when you say to a man whom you are rebuking and reproaching: "You did this, you did this?" It is also possible that the repetition is because He described him in each verse with something additional to what He described him with in the other verse. It is as if He said: "And among mankind is one who disputes about God and follows every rebellious devil without knowledge, ﴿and without guidance or an illuminating Book﴾, in order to lead astray from the way of God." End of quotation. It has also been said that the first verse concerns those who imitate (muqallidūn) in the form of the active participle, and the second concerns those who are imitated in the form of the passive participle. The second is general to every act of misleading and disputing. The accusative of ﴿turning his side﴾ is a ḥāl from the subject of "disputes." ʿIṭf means the side, and the two ʿiṭfs of a man are his two sides, right and left. There are two views on its interpretation. The first is that it means one who twists his neck out of insolence and arrogance. al-Zajjaj mentioned this meaning and said: "This is how the arrogant person is described." The meaning is: among mankind is one who disputes about God arrogantly. al-Mubarrad said: "ʿIṭf is the part of the neck that is bent." The second view is that His words ﴿turning his side﴾ mean turning away: that is, turning away from the remembrance. This was said by al-Farra', al-Mufaḍḍal, and others, as in His words: ﴿He turned away arrogantly as if he had not heard it﴾ [Luqman: 7], His words ﴿They turned their heads﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 5], and His words ﴿He turned away and withdrew with his side﴾ [al-Isra': 83]. The lam in ﴿in order to lead astray from the way of God﴾ is connected to "disputes": that is, his aim is to lead astray from the way, even if he does not admit it. It was read as "li-yaḍilla" (with a fatḥa on the yāʾ), in which case the lam is the lam of consequence (lam al-ʿāqibah), as if He made his going astray the end of his disputing. The clause ﴿For him in this world is disgrace﴾ is a new (resumed) sentence explaining what results for him from his disputing, namely the punishment. Khizy means humiliation. This is by the punishment he receives in this world, which is the hastened torment and evil mention on people's tongues. It has been said that the worldly disgrace is death, as happened on the day of Badr. ﴿And We will make him taste on the Day of Resurrection the punishment of the burning﴾, that is, the punishment of the burning Fire. The bāʾ is causal: that is, that punishment which descends upon you is because of what your hands have sent forth of disbelief and sins. He expressed the whole body by "hands" because the commission of sins is generally done with them. The discussion of this verse has already passed at the end of Al ʿImran, so we will not repeat it.

The one who worships God on a harf is restless in his religion, without firmness and tranquility, like one who is on the edge of a mountain or the like, who shakes violently and whose standing weakens. So the one who doubts his religion is said to worship God on a harf, because he is not certain of His promise and threat, unlike the believer, who worships Him with certainty and insight, so he is not on a harf. It has also been said: the harf is a condition, meaning: among mankind is one who worships God on a condition, and the condition is His words ﴿If good befalls him, he is content with it﴾, that is, worldly good of prosperity, well-being, abundance, and much wealth. The meaning of "is content with it" is that he remains firm in his religion and persists in his worship, or that his heart is at rest with that good which has befallen him. ﴿But if an ordeal befalls him﴾, that is, something by which he is tested, of a disliked kind that afflicts him in his family, his property, or himself, ﴿he turns over on his face﴾, that is, he apostatizes and returns to the state of disbelief he had been in. Then He described his condition after his turning over on his face, saying: ﴿He has lost this world and the Hereafter﴾, that is, he has gone and lost both. So he has no share in this world of spoils and good repute, nor in the Hereafter of reward and what God has prepared for His righteous servants. Mujahid, Humayd ibn Qays, al-Aʿraj, al-Zuhri, and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "khasira" in the form of the active participle, "khasiran al-dunya wa'l-akhirah," in the accusative as a ḥāl. It was also read in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject. The demonstrative in His words "that" refers to the loss of this world and the Hereafter, and it is the subject, with its predicate ﴿that is the manifest loss﴾, that is, the clear, evident loss to which there is no equal. ﴿He calls upon, besides God, that which neither harms him nor benefits him﴾, that is, this one who turned over on his face and returned to disbelief calls upon, besides God, meaning he worships, going beyond the worship of God to the worship of idols, that which does not harm him if he abandons its worship, nor benefit him if he worships it, because that object of worship is inanimate and has no power over harm or benefit. The demonstrative in His words "that" refers to the calling, which is understood from the verb "he calls," and the demonstrative is a subject whose predicate is ﴿That is the far-off error﴾, that is, far from truth and right guidance. It is a metaphor taken from the error of one who goes by other than the road and, by his error, becomes far from it. al-Farra' said: "Baʿid" means long.

﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾. "Yadʿu" here means "yaqūlu" (says). The clause confirms what precedes it, namely that this calling is far-off error. Idols have no benefit in them in any way at all; rather, they are pure harm to the one who worships them, because he has entered the Fire because of worshipping them. The use of the comparative form, despite the total absence of benefit, is for emphasis in disparaging the condition of that caller, or it is of the kind of His words ﴿Indeed, we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Saba': 24]. The lam is the one preparing for the oath (al-lām al-muwaṭṭiʾah lil-qasam), and "man" is a relative pronoun or a qualifying noun. "Darruhu" is the subject, whose predicate is "aqrabu," and the clause is the relative clause. The clause ﴿Surely the worst patron and the worst companion﴾ is the answer to the oath. The meaning is: that disbeliever will say that on the Day of Resurrection to the one he worshipped, whose harm is nearer than his benefit: "Worst is the patron you are, and worst is the companion." al-Mawla is the helper, and al-ʿashir is the companion. Like what is in this verse is the saying of ʿAntarah:

They call on ʿAntarah while the spears are like the ropes of a well
in the chest of the dark-coloured horse.

al-Zajjaj said: It is possible that "yadʿu" is in the position of a ḥāl, and in it there is an omitted pronoun, meaning: that is the far-off error, he calls it. In this case one stops at "yadʿu," and His words ﴿for him whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾ form a new sentence, nominative by the inception, whose predicate is "la-bi'sa al-mawla" (surely worst is the patron). He said: This is because the lam is for the oath and emphasis, so he placed it at the beginning of the sentence.

al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' said: It is possible that "yadʿu" is repeated upon what precedes it, as an intensification of this action, which is calling: that is, he calls upon what neither harms him nor benefits him, he calls. Like "I struck Zayd, I struck." al-Farra', al-Kisa'i, and al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of the sentence is an oath, and the lam is placed before its proper position, and the estimate is: "He calls upon whoever surely whose harm is nearer than his benefit." So "man" is in the accusative position governed by "yadʿu," the lam is the answer to the oath, "darruhu" is the subject, and "aqrabu" is its predicate. Among the rearrangements of the lam by fronting and postponing is the poet's saying:

My uncle, you surely are, and whoever Jarir is his uncle,
will attain glory and honour the maternal uncles.

That is: "Surely you are my uncle." al-Nahhas said: ʿAli ibn Sulayman related to us from Muhammad ibn Yazid, who said: "There is an omission in the sentence, and the meaning is: he calls upon for whoever's harm is nearer than his benefit a god." al-Nahhas said: I think this statement is a mistake from Muhammad ibn Yazid, and perhaps its basis is that what comes before this lam does not govern what comes after it. al-Farra' also and al-Qaffal said: the lam is a ṣilah, that is, superfluous, and the meaning is: he calls upon whoever's harm is nearer than his benefit, that is, he worships him. Likewise in the reading of ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, with the lam omitted. On this view the lam in "la-bi'sa al-mawla" and in "la-bi'sa al-ʿashir" is the one preparing for the oath.

﴿Indeed, God will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. When He finished mentioning the condition of the polytheists, and of the one who worships God on a harf, He mentioned the condition of the believers in the Hereafter, and informed that He will admit them into these gardens which have this description. The discussion of rivers flowing beneath them has already passed, and it is clear. If by "gardens" is meant the land, then a genitive noun must be estimated: that is, beneath its trees. ﴿Indeed, God does what He wills﴾. This sentence is a reason for what precedes it: that is, He does what He wills of acts, ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ [al-Anbiya': 23], so He rewards whom He wills and punishes whom He wills.

﴿Whoever thinks that God will not help him in this world and the Hereafter﴾. al-Nahhas said: Among the best things said about this verse is that the meaning is: whoever thinks that God will not help Muhammad, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, and that it is possible for him to cut off the help that he has been given. ﴿Let him stretch a rope to the sky﴾, that is, let him seek a means by which he reaches the sky, then let him cut, that is, then let him cut off the help if it is possible for him. ﴿Then let him look: will his scheme remove what enrages him?﴾ His scheme and stratagem is what enrages him of the help of the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace. It has been said that the meaning is: whoever thinks that God will not help Muhammad until He makes him prevail over all religion, then let him die of rage. Then he explained it by His words ﴿Let him stretch a rope to the sky﴾, that is, let him tie a rope to the ceiling of his house. ﴿Then let him cut﴾, that is, then let him pull the rope until it breaks, so that he dies strangled. The meaning is: let him choke with rage until he dies, for God is his helper and the one who makes him prevail, and his rage will not benefit him. The meaning of "then let him look: will his scheme remove what enrages him?" is: his action and stratagem, what enrages, that is, his rage; "ma" is a verbal noun (maṣdariyyah). It has been said that the pronoun in "yanṣuruhu" refers to "man," and the meaning is: whoever thinks that God does not provide for him, let him kill himself, and Abu ʿUbaydah said this. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the religion: that is, whoever thinks that God will not help His religion. The Kufans read "thumma li-yaqṭaʿ" with the lam of the imperative sukūn. al-Nahhas said: This reading is far from the Arabic language.

It was also read in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject. The demonstrative in His words "that" refers to the loss of this world and the Hereafter, and it is the subject, with its predicate ﴿that is the manifest loss﴾, that is, the clear, evident loss to which there is no equal. ﴿He calls upon, besides God, that which neither harms him nor benefits him﴾, that is, this one who turned over on his face and returned to disbelief calls upon, besides God, meaning he worships, going beyond the worship of God to the worship of idols, that which does not harm him if he abandons its worship, nor benefit him if he worships it, because that object of worship is inanimate and has no power over harm or benefit. The demonstrative in His words "that" refers to the calling, which is understood from the verb "he calls," and the demonstrative is a subject whose predicate is ﴿That is the far-off error﴾, that is, far from truth and right guidance. It is a metaphor taken from the error of one who goes by other than the road and, by his error, becomes far from it. al-Farra' said: "Baʿid" means long.

﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾. "Yadʿu" here means "yaqūlu" (says). The clause confirms what precedes it, namely that this calling is far-off error. Idols have no benefit in them in any way at all; rather, they are pure harm to the one who worships them, because he has entered the Fire because of worshipping them. The use of the comparative form, despite the total absence of benefit, is for emphasis in disparaging the condition of that caller, or it is of the kind of His words ﴿Indeed, we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Saba': 24]. The lam is the one preparing for the oath (al-lām al-muwaṭṭiʾah lil-qasam), and "man" is a relative pronoun or a qualifying noun. "Darruhu" is the subject, whose predicate is "aqrabu," and the clause is the relative clause. The clause ﴿Surely the worst patron and the worst companion﴾ is the answer to the oath. The meaning is: that disbeliever will say that on the Day of Resurrection to the one he worshipped, whose harm is nearer than his benefit: "Worst is the patron you are, and worst is the companion." al-Mawla is the helper, and al-ʿashir is the companion. Like what is in this verse is the saying of ʿAntarah:

They call on ʿAntarah while the spears are like the ropes of a well
in the chest of the dark-coloured horse.

al-Zajjaj said: It is possible that "yadʿu" is in the position of a ḥāl, and in it there is an omitted pronoun, meaning: that is the far-off error, he calls it. In this case one stops at "yadʿu," and His words ﴿for him whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾ form a new sentence, nominative by the inception, whose predicate is "la-bi'sa al-mawla" (surely worst is the patron). He said: This is because the lam is for the oath and emphasis, so he placed it at the beginning of the sentence.

My uncle, you surely are, and whoever Jarir is his uncle,
will attain glory and honour the maternal uncles.

That is: "Surely you are my uncle." al-Nahhas said: ʿAli ibn Sulayman related to us from Muhammad ibn Yazid, who said: "There is an omission in the sentence, and the meaning is: he calls upon for whoever's harm is nearer than his benefit a god." al-Nahhas said: I think this statement is a mistake from Muhammad ibn Yazid, and perhaps its basis is that what comes before this lam does not govern what comes after it. al-Farra' also and al-Qaffal said: the lam is a ṣilah, that is, superfluous, and the meaning is: he calls upon whoever's harm is nearer than his benefit, that is, he worships him. Thus We have sent it down as clear signs, meaning: in the same wondrous manner of sending down, We have sent it down as clear signs whose indications are evident in what they signify. ﴿And that Allah guides whom He wills﴾, meaning whose guidance He wills, either initially or by increasing it for one who was already guided before.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse that he said: "He is a man from the Banu ʿAbd al-Dar."

But if his wife did not bear and his mares did not foal, he would say, 'This is a bad religion.'"

Ibn Abi Ḥatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him, with a sound chain, that he said: "Some Bedouins would come to the Prophet (ﷺ) and embrace Islam. When they returned to their lands, if they found a year of rain, a year of fertility and a year of good births, they would say, 'Indeed, this religion of ours is good, so hold fast to it.' But if they found a year of drought, a year of bad births and a year of famine, they would say, 'There is nothing good in this religion of ours.' So Allah revealed: ﴿And among the people is one who worships Allah on an edge﴾."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Ḥatim and Ibn Mardawayh also reported from him something similar, and in its chain is al-ʿAwfi.

Ibn Mardawayh also reported through the same route from Abu Saʿid that he said: "A man from the Jews embraced Islam, then he lost his sight, his wealth and his child, so he considered Islam an ill omen. He came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said, 'Release me, release me!' He (ﷺ) said, 'Islam cannot be relinquished.' The man said, 'I have gained nothing good from this religion of mine: I lost my sight, my wealth, and my child died.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said, 'O Jew, Islam refines men as fire refines the dross of iron, gold and silver.' So there was revealed: ﴿And among the people is one who worships Allah on an edge﴾."
