Al-Azhari said: that is, they will be prepared and made into a garment for them. The fire was likened to garments, because it envelops them as garments envelop. He expressed the future by the past to indicate the certainty of its occurrence. It has been said: these garments are of brass that has been melted so that it becomes like fire, and they are the "sarabil" (garments) mentioned in another verse. It has been said: the meaning in the verse is: the fire has encompassed them. It was read "qutti'at" (قُطِعَتْ) with lightening (qutti'at, not qutti'at). Then He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Boiling water will be poured over their heads﴾. The ḥamīm is hot water boiled by the fire of Jahannam, and the clause is either resumptive or is a second predicate of the relative pronoun.

﴿By which that which is in their bellies will be melted﴾. Al-ṣahr is melting, and al-ṣuhāra is what has melted from it. It is said: "ṣahartu al-shay'a fanṣahara," meaning: I melted the thing and it melted, so it is ṣahīr. The meaning is that by that boiling water will be melted what is in their bellies of intestines, viscera and skins. "Skins" is coordinated with "mā": meaning, and the skins will be melted by it. The clause is in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). It has been said: the skins are not melted but burned, so a verb suitable to that is estimated, and it is said: "and the skins will be burned by it," as in the saying of the poet: "I fed her straw and cold water," meaning: and I gave her water to drink. It is not hidden that there is no need for this, for if the ḥamīm melts what is in the bellies, then its melting of the outer skin is more fitting.

﴿And for them are maqāmi' of iron﴾. The maqāmi' is the plural of maqma'ah, and maq'ma'a: I struck him with the miqma'ah, which is a piece of iron. The meaning: for them are maqāmi' of iron with which they will be struck, that is, the disbelievers. The maqāmi' were named maqāmi' because they subdue the one struck, that is, they humiliate him. Ibn al-Sikkit said: "aqma'tu al-rajula 'anni iqma'an" means: when he came upon you and you turned him back from you.

﴿Whenever they wish to come out from it﴾, that is, from the Fire, they will be returned into it, that is, into the Fire, by striking with the maqāmi'. "From grief" (min ghammin) is a substitute for the pronoun in "minha" by repeating the preposition, or it is an object of purpose: meaning, because of a severe grief from the griefs of the Fire. ﴿And taste the punishment of the burning﴾: it is by estimating a saying: that is, they will be returned into it, and it was said: it is said to them: taste the punishment of the burning, that is, the burning punishment. The original meaning of al-ḥarīq is the noun of burning; one burns a thing with fire, and it burns, a burning, and a combustion. Dhawq (tasting) is a contact by which the perception of taste is attained, and it is used here figuratively, and what is meant by it is the perception of pain. Al-Zajjaj said: this is for one of the two adversaries, and he said of the other adversary, who are the believers:

﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who believed and did righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. Thus He, glorified is He, explained the state of the believers after His explanation of the state of the disbelievers. Then Allah, glorified is He, explained some of what He has prepared for them of bliss after their entry into the Garden, and said: ﴿They will be adorned therein﴾. The majority read "yuḥallawna" (يُحَلَّونَ) with doubling and the passive voice, and it was read without doubling: meaning, Allah or the angels by His command will adorn them. "Min" in His saying "min asāwira" (مِن أساوِرَ) is partitive: meaning, they will be adorned with some bracelets; or explanatory; or superfluous. "Min" in "min dhahabin" (مِن ذَهَبٍ) is explanatory. The asāwir are the plural of uswah, and uswah is the plural of siwār, and for siwār there are two dialects: with kasr of the sīn and with ḍamm of it, and there is a third dialect, which is asār. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Asim and Shaybah read "wa-lu'lu'an" (ولُؤْلُؤًا) with the accusative, coordinated with the position of "asāwira": meaning, and they will be adorned with pearls; or by an estimated verb governing its accusative. Likewise Ya'qub, al-Ju'dari and Isa ibn Umar read it with the accusative, and this reading is the one that agrees with the orthography of the Mushaf, since this word is written in it with an alif. The rest read it in the genitive, coordinated with "asāwira": meaning, they will be adorned with bracelets of gold and of pearls. It is not far-fetched that in the Garden there is a bracelet of solid pearl, just as there are bracelets of gold in it.

﴿And their clothing therein is silk﴾: meaning, all that they wear is silk, as this idāfah (construction) indicates. It is also possible that what is meant is that this kind of clothing which was forbidden to them in the world is lawful for them in the Hereafter, and that it is among what they wear there. Thus, in it is what the souls desire, and each one of them is given what his soul desires and attains what he wishes.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 22, verse 17–24 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And they were guided to the good word﴾, i.e., they were guided to it. It has been said it is "There is no god but Allah." It has been said: "Praise be to Allah." It has been said: the Qur'an. It has been said: it is what comes to them from Allah, glorified is He, of good tidings. The Qur'an has indicated what supports this general statement here, namely His saying, glorified is He: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us﴾ [al-Zumar: 74]; ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has guided us to this﴾ [al-A'raf: 43]; ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has removed from us grief﴾ [Fatir: 34]. The meaning of ﴿and they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy﴾ is that they were guided to the praiseworthy path, which is the way to Paradise, or the path of Allah, which is His upright religion, namely Islam.

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿and the Sabians﴾, that he said: they are a people who worship the angels, pray towards the qiblah, and recite the Zabur. ﴿And the Magians﴾ are worshippers of the sun, the moon and the fires. ﴿And those who associated partners﴾ are worshippers of idols. ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them﴾: he said, "The religions are six: five belong to Satan, and the religion of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is one."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Ikrimah regarding the verse that he said: "He decided His judgment between them, so He made the five shared, and made this nation one."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Those who were Jews: the Jews. The Sabians: they have no book. The Magians: the people of idols. And the polytheists: the Christians of the Arabs."

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Abu Dharr that he used to swear an oath that this verse ﴿These two adversaries dispute﴾ up to the end of the verse was revealed concerning the three and the three who fought at the Battle of Badr: Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, 'Ubaydah ibn al-Harith, and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib on one side, and 'Utbah and Shaybah, the sons of Rabi'ah, and al-Walid ibn 'Utbah on the other. 'Ali said: "I will be the first to kneel in dispute before Allah on the Day of Resurrection." al-Bukhari and others related it from the hadith of 'Ali. Ibn Mardawayh related it from Ibn 'Abbas with similar wording, and it has been related likewise from a group of the Followers.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding His saying ﴿Garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾, that he said: "of brass; and there is nothing among vessels that, when heated, is more intensely hot than it." Regarding His saying ﴿Boiling water will be poured over their heads﴾, he said: "the brass will be melted over their heads." His saying ﴿By which what is in their bellies will be melted, and the skins﴾, he said: "their intestines will flow out," and "the skins" – he said: "their skins will be stripped off."

'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sahih, 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Zuhd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who graded it sahih, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Hurayrah that he recited this verse ﴿Boiling water will be poured over their heads﴾ and said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Indeed the boiling water will be poured over their heads, and it will penetrate the skull until it reaches the inside, and it will melt what is in the belly until it passes out through the feet, and that is the melting (al-sahr), and then it will be restored as it was."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿By which what is in their bellies will be melted﴾, that he said: "They walk while their intestines are falling out and their skins."

And regarding His saying ﴿And for them are maqami' of iron﴾, he said: "They will be struck with them, so that each limb falls in its place, and they will call out for destruction and ruin." Ibn Jarir related from him regarding the verse that he said: "They will be given water which, when it enters their bellies, melts them, and the skins along with the bellies."

Ahmad, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who graded it sahih, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th wal-Nushur related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "If a maqma' of iron were placed in the earth and all of mankind and jinn gathered to lift it, they would not be able to lift it from the earth; and if a mountain were struck with a maqma' of iron, it would be shattered and then return as it was."

Ibn al-Mubarak, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Hannad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who graded it sahih, related from Salman, who said: "The Fire is black and dark; its flame does not give light, nor its embers." Then he recited: ﴿Every time they wish to come out of it, out of distress, they will be returned into it﴾.

In the Two Sahihs and others, from 'Umar, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever wears silk in this world will not wear it in the Hereafter." There are other hadiths on this subject.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And they were guided to the good word﴾, that he said: "They were inspired." Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-'Aliyah, who said: "They were guided to the good word in disputing when they said: 'Allah is our Protector, and you have no protector.'" Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid regarding the verse that he said: "The Qur'an." ﴿And they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy﴾: "Islam." Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi (p-960) Hatim related from al-Dahhak regarding the verse that he said: "Islam." Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Zayd, who said: "There is no god but Allah, Allah is greatest, and all praise is due to Allah, who said: ﴿To Him ascends the good word﴾ [Fatir: 10]."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 22, verses 17–24 (part 1 of 2):

.
His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾, meaning in Allah and His Messenger, or in what has been mentioned of the clear signs. ﴿And those who are Jews﴾ are the Jews who ascribe themselves to the religion of Musa (Moses). The Sabians are a people who worship the stars. It has also been said that they are of the same kind as the Christians, but this is not correct. Rather, they are a well-known sect that does not trace back to any of the religions ascribed to the prophets. The Christians are those who ascribe themselves to the religion of Isa (Jesus). The Magians are those who worship fire and say that the world has two origins: light and darkness. It has also been said that they worship the sun and the moon. It has been said that they use impurities. It has been said that they are a group of Christians who withdrew from them and wore woolen garments. It has also been said that they took part of the religion of the Jews and part of the religion of the Christians. ﴿And those who associate partners﴾ are those who worship idols. The verification of this has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah, but there He, glorified is He, placed the Christians before the Sabians, and here He placed them after them. It has been said that the reason for placing the Christians first there is that they are a people of a Book, unlike the Sabians, and the reason for placing the Sabians first here is that their era precedes the era of the Christians. The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ is in the position of a nominative, being the predicate (khabar) of the preceding inna (the particle of emphasis). The meaning of judging is that He, glorified is He, will decide between them, admitting the believers among them (p-958) into the Garden and the disbelievers among them into the Fire. It has been said that judging is that the truthful is distinguished from the falsehood by a sign by which each of the two is recognized. The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things a witness﴾ is a justification of what precedes it, meaning: He, glorified is He, is a witness over all things, of the actions and the sayings of His creatures; nothing of them is hidden from Him. Al-Farra' denied that the clause ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them﴾ could be a predicate of the preceding inna. He said: it is not permissible in speech to say: "Inna Zaydan inna akhahu muntaliqun" (Indeed Zayd, indeed his brother is departing). Al-Zajjaj refuted what al-Farra' said, and rejected it, and rejected what he made similar to the verse. There is no doubt about the permissibility of your saying: "Inna Zaydan al-khayru 'indahu" (Indeed Zayd, the good is with him), and "Inna Zaydan innahu muntaliqun" (Indeed Zayd, indeed he is departing), and the like.

﴿Have you not seen that to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth﴾. The seeing here is of the heart, not of the eye: meaning, have you not known? The address is to everyone who is fit for it, that is, whoever is capable of seeing. The intended meaning of prostration here is complete submission, not the prostration of worship that is specific to the rational beings, whether the word "man" (whoever) is taken as specific to rational beings or as general to them and to others. For this reason He joined ﴿and the sun, and the moon, and the stars, and the mountains, and the trees, and the moving creatures﴾ to "whoever", since that indicates that the prostration is submission and not the worship specific to the rational beings. He singled out these matters for mention, although they are included under "whoever", on the assumption that it is general, because prostration by them is unusual in custom. The raising of ﴿and many of the people﴾ is by an implied verb indicated by what is mentioned, meaning: and many of the people prostrate to Him. It has been said that it is raised as a beginning (mubtada'), and its predicate is omitted, its estimate being: "and many of the people deserve reward." The first is more evident. It was not raised by coordination with "whoever" because the prostration of this great number of people is the prostration of worship specific to the rational beings, while the prostration mentioned earlier is submission. Had it been raised by coordination with "whoever", that would have combined two different meanings in one word. You know that there is no need for this after understanding prostration as submission, and there is no doubt that it is valid to mean by the prostration of many of the people their submission, not the specific prostration itself. So raising it by coordination is not objectionable, even though the author of al-Kashshaf (Zamakhshari) and his followers refused it. As for His saying: ﴿and many deserve the punishment﴾, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: it is raised as a beginning, and its predicate is what follows it. It has been said: it is coordinated with the first "many", and the meaning is: "and many of the people prostrate, and many of them refuse that." It has been said: the meaning is: "and many of the people are in the Garden, and many deserve the punishment." Ibn al-Anbari related it in this way.

﴿And whoever Allah humiliates, there is for him no honorer﴾: meaning, whoever Allah has humiliated by making him a disbeliever, a wretch, then there is for him no honorer who honors him, so he becomes fortunate and mighty. Al-Akhfash, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' related that the meaning is: ﴿and whoever Allah humiliates, there is for him no honorer﴾: that is, no honoring. ﴿Indeed, Allah does what He wills﴾ of the things, of which among them is what has preceded mention of wretchedness, happiness, honor and humiliation.

﴿These two adversaries (khasmani) have disputed﴾. The two adversaries: one of them is the most impure of the groups, namely the Jews, the Christians, the Sabians, the Magians and those who associate partners; and the other adversary is the Muslims. Thus they are two parties in dispute. This was said by al-Farra' and others. It has been said: the intended meaning of the two adversaries is the Garden and the Fire. The Garden said: "He created me for His mercy," and the Fire said: "He created me for His punishment." It has been said: the intended meaning of the two adversaries is those who came forth on the Day of Badr: from the believers, Hamzah, Ali and Ubaydah; and from the disbelievers, Utbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabi'ah, and al-Walid ibn Utbah. Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, used to swear that this verse was revealed concerning these challengers, as is established from him in the Sahih, and a group of the Companions said the like of this, and they know the causes of revelation better than others. It is also established in the Sahih from Ali that he said: "It was concerning us that this verse was revealed." Ibn Kathir read "Hadhani" (هَذانِّ) with a doubled nun, and He, glorified is He, said "they disputed" (ikhtasamu) and did not say "ikhtasama" (the dual). The meaning of "in their Lord" (fi rabbihim) is: in the matter of their Lord, that is, in His religion, or in His essence, or in His attributes, or in His legislation for His servants, or in all of that. 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sahih, 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Zuhd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who graded it sahih, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Hurayrah that he recited this verse ﴿Boiling water will be poured over their heads﴾ and said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Indeed the boiling water will be poured over their heads, and it will penetrate the skull until it reaches the inside, and it will melt what is in the belly until it passes out through the feet, and that is the melting (al-sahr), and then it will be restored as it was."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿By which what is in their bellies will be melted﴾, that he said: "They walk while their intestines are falling out and their skins."

And regarding His saying ﴿And for them are maqami' of iron﴾, he said: "They will be struck with them, so that each limb falls in its place, and they will call out for destruction and ruin." Ibn Jarir related from him regarding the verse that he said: "They will be given water which, when it enters their bellies, melts them, and the skins along with the bellies."

Ahmad, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who graded it sahih, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th wal-Nushur related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "If a maqma' of iron were placed in the earth and all of mankind and jinn gathered to lift it, they would not be able to lift it from the earth; and if a mountain were struck with a maqma' of iron, it would be shattered and then return as it was."

Ibn al-Mubarak, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Hannad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who graded it sahih, related from Salman, who said: "The Fire is black and dark; its flame does not give light, nor its embers." Then he recited: ﴿Every time they wish to come out of it, out of distress, they will be returned into it﴾.

In the Two Sahihs and others, from 'Umar, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever wears silk in this world will not wear it in the Hereafter." There are other hadiths on this subject.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And they were guided to the good word﴾, that he said: "They were inspired." Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-'Aliyah, who said: "They were guided to the good word in disputing when they said: 'Allah is our Protector, and you have no protector.'" Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid regarding the verse that he said: "The Qur'an." ﴿And they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy﴾: "Islam." Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi (p-960) Hatim related from al-Dahhak regarding the verse that he said: "Islam." Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Zayd, who said: "There is no god but Allah, Allah is greatest, and all praise is due to Allah, who said: ﴿To Him ascends the good word﴾ [Fatir: 10]."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 22, verses 17–24 (part 1 of 2):

.
His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾, meaning in Allah and His Messenger, or in what has been mentioned of the clear signs. ﴿And those who are Jews﴾ are the Jews who ascribe themselves to the religion of Musa (Moses). The Sabians are a people who worship the stars. It has also been said that they are of the same kind as the Christians, but this is not correct. Rather, they are a well-known sect that does not trace back to any of the religions ascribed to the prophets. The Christians are those who ascribe themselves to the religion of Isa (Jesus). The Magians are those who worship fire and say that the world has two origins: light and darkness. It has also been said that they worship the sun and the moon. It has been said that they use impurities. It has been said that they are a group of Christians who withdrew from them and wore woolen garments. It has also been said that they took part of the religion of the Jews and part of the religion of the Christians. ﴿And those who associate partners﴾ are those who worship idols. The verification of this has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah, but there He, glorified is He, placed the Christians before the Sabians, and here He placed them after them. It has been said that the reason for placing the Christians first there is that they are a people of a Book, unlike the Sabians, and the reason for placing the Sabians first here is that their era precedes the era of the Christians. The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ is in the position of a nominative, being the predicate (khabar) of the preceding inna (the particle of emphasis). The meaning of judging is that He, glorified is He, will decide between them, admitting the believers among them (p-958) into the Garden and the disbelievers among them into the Fire. It has been said that judging is that the truthful is distinguished from the falsehood by a sign by which each of the two is recognized. The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things a witness﴾ is a justification of what precedes it, meaning: He, glorified is He, is a witness over all things, of the actions and the sayings of His creatures; nothing of them is hidden from Him. Al-Farra' denied that the clause ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them﴾ could be a predicate of the preceding inna. He said: it is not permissible in speech to say: "Inna Zaydan inna akhahu muntaliqun" (Indeed Zayd, indeed his brother is departing). Al-Zajjaj refuted what al-Farra' said, and rejected it, and rejected what he made similar to the verse. There is no doubt about the permissibility of your saying: "Inna Zaydan al-khayru 'indahu" (Indeed Zayd, the good is with him), and "Inna Zaydan innahu muntaliqun" (Indeed Zayd, indeed he is departing), and the like.

﴿Have you not seen that to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth﴾. The seeing here is of the heart, not of the eye: meaning, have you not known? The address is to everyone who is fit for it, that is, whoever is capable of seeing. The intended meaning of prostration here is complete submission, not the prostration of worship that is specific to the rational beings, whether the word "man" (whoever) is taken as specific to rational beings or as general to them and to others. For this reason He joined ﴿and the sun, and the moon, and the stars, and the mountains, and the trees, and the moving creatures﴾ to "whoever", since that indicates that the prostration is submission and not the worship specific to the rational beings. He singled out these matters for mention, although they are included under "whoever", on the assumption that it is general, because prostration by them is unusual in custom. The raising of ﴿and many of the people﴾ is by an implied verb indicated by what is mentioned, meaning: and many of the people prostrate to Him. It has been said that it is raised as a beginning (mubtada'), and its predicate is omitted, its estimate being: "and many of the people deserve reward." The first is more evident. It was not raised by coordination with "whoever" because the prostration of this great number of people is the prostration of worship specific to the rational beings, while the prostration mentioned earlier is submission. Had it been raised by coordination with "whoever", that would have combined two different meanings in one word. You know that there is no need for this after understanding prostration as submission, and there is no doubt that it is valid to mean by the prostration of many of the people their submission, not the specific prostration itself. So raising it by coordination is not objectionable, even though the author of al-Kashshaf (Zamakhshari) and his followers refused it. As for His saying: ﴿and many deserve the punishment﴾, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: it is raised as a beginning, and its predicate is what follows it. It has been said: it is coordinated with the first "many", and the meaning is: "and many of the people prostrate, and many of them refuse that." It has been said: the meaning is: "and many of the people are in the Garden, and many deserve the punishment." Ibn al-Anbari related it in this way.

﴿And whoever Allah humiliates, there is for him no honorer﴾: meaning, whoever Allah has humiliated by making him a disbeliever, a wretch, then there is for him no honorer who honors him, so he becomes fortunate and mighty. Al-Akhfash, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' related that the meaning is: ﴿and whoever Allah humiliates, there is for him no honorer﴾: that is, no honoring. ﴿Indeed, Allah does what He wills﴾ of the things, of which among them is what has preceded mention of wretchedness, happiness, honor and humiliation.

﴿These two adversaries (khasmani) have disputed﴾. The two adversaries: one of them is the most impure of the groups, namely the Jews, the Christians, the Sabians, the Magians and those who associate partners; and the other adversary is the Muslims. Thus they are two parties in dispute. This was said by al-Farra' and others. It has been said: the intended meaning of the two adversaries is the Garden and the Fire. The Garden said: "He created me for His mercy," and the Fire said: "He created me for His punishment." It has been said: the intended meaning of the two adversaries is those who came forth on the Day of Badr: from the believers, Hamzah, Ali and Ubaydah; and from the disbelievers, Utbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabi'ah, and al-Walid ibn Utbah. Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, used to swear that this verse was revealed concerning these challengers, as is established from him in the Sahih, and a group of the Companions said the like of this, and they know the causes of revelation better than others. It is also established in the Sahih from Ali that he said: "It was concerning us that this verse was revealed." Ibn Kathir read "Hadhani" (هَذانِّ) with a doubled nun, and He, glorified is He, said "they disputed" (ikhtasamu) and did not say "ikhtasama" (the dual). Al-Farra' said: because they are a plural group; had He said "ikhtasama" it would have been permissible. The meaning of "in their Lord" (fi rabbihim) is: in the matter of their Lord, that is, in His religion, or in His essence, or in His attributes, or in His legislation for His servants, or in all of that. Then He, glorified is He, explained what He had summarized in His saying ﴿He will judge between them﴾, and said: ﴿As for those who disbelieved, garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾. Al-Azhari said: that is, they will be prepared and made into a garment for them. The fire was likened to garments, because it envelops them as garments envelop. He expressed the future by the past to indicate the certainty of its occurrence. It has been said: these garments are of brass that has been melted so that it becomes like fire, and they are the "sarabil" (garments) mentioned in another verse. It has been said: the meaning in the verse is: the fire has encompassed them. It was read "qutti'at" (قُطِعَتْ) with lightening (qutti'at, not qutti'at). Then He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Boiling water will be poured over their heads﴾. The ḥamīm is hot water boiled by the fire of Jahannam, and the clause is either resumptive or is a second predicate of the relative pronoun.

﴿By which that which is in their bellies will be melted﴾. Al-ṣahr is melting, and al-ṣuhāra is what has melted from it. It is said: "ṣahartu al-shay'a fanṣahara," meaning: I melted the thing and it melted, so it is ṣahīr. The meaning is that by that boiling water will be melted what is in their bellies of intestines, viscera and skins. "Skins" is coordinated with "mā": meaning, and the skins will be melted by it. The clause is in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). It has been said: the skins are not melted but burned, so a verb suitable to that is estimated, and it is said: "and the skins will be burned by it," as in the saying of the poet: "I fed her straw and cold water," meaning: and I gave her water to drink. It is not hidden that there is no need for this, for if the ḥamīm melts what is in the bellies, then its melting of the outer skin is more fitting.

﴿And for them are maqāmi' of iron﴾. The maqāmi' is the plural of maqma'ah, and maq'ma'a: I struck him with the miqma'ah, which is a piece of iron. The meaning: for them are maqāmi' of iron with which they will be struck, that is, the disbelievers. The maqāmi' were named maqāmi' because they subdue the one struck, that is, they humiliate him. Ibn al-Sikkit said: "aqma'tu al-rajula 'anni iqma'an" means: when he came upon you and you turned him back from you.

﴿Whenever they wish to come out from it﴾, that is, from the Fire, they will be returned into it, that is, into the Fire, by striking with the maqāmi'. "From grief" (min ghammin) is a substitute for the pronoun in "minha" by repeating the preposition, or it is an object of purpose: meaning, because of a severe grief from the griefs of the Fire. ﴿And taste the punishment of the burning﴾: it is by estimating a saying: that is, they will be returned into it, and it was said: it is said to them: taste the punishment of the burning, that is, the burning punishment. The original meaning of al-ḥarīq is the noun of burning; one burns a thing with fire, and it burns, a burning, and a combustion. Dhawq (tasting) is a contact by which the perception of taste is attained, and it is used here figuratively, and what is meant by it is the perception of pain. Al-Zajjaj said: this is for one of the two adversaries, and he said of the other adversary, who are the believers:

﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who believed and did righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. Thus He, glorified is He, explained the state of the believers after His explanation of the state of the disbelievers. Then Allah, glorified is He, explained some of what He has prepared for them of bliss after their entry into the Garden, and said: ﴿They will be adorned therein﴾. The majority read "yuḥallawna" (يُحَلَّونَ) with doubling and the passive voice, and it was read without doubling: meaning, Allah or the angels by His command will adorn them. "Min" in His saying "min asāwira" (مِن أساوِرَ) is partitive: meaning, they will be adorned with some bracelets; or explanatory; or superfluous. "Min" in "min dhahabin" (مِن ذَهَبٍ) is explanatory. The asāwir are the plural of uswah, and uswah is the plural of siwār, and for siwār there are two dialects: with kasr of the sīn and with ḍamm of it, and there is a third dialect, which is asār. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Asim and Shaybah read "wa-lu'lu'an" (ولُؤْلُؤًا) with the accusative, coordinated with the position of "asāwira": meaning, and they will be adorned with pearls; or by an estimated verb governing its accusative. Likewise Ya'qub, al-Ju'dari and Isa ibn Umar read it with the accusative, and this reading is the one that agrees with the orthography of the Mushaf, since this word is written in it with an alif. The rest read it in the genitive, coordinated with "asāwira": meaning, they will be adorned with bracelets of gold and of pearls. It is not far-fetched that in the Garden there is a bracelet of solid pearl, just as there are bracelets of gold in it.

﴿And their clothing therein is silk﴾: meaning, all that they wear is silk, as this idāfah (construction) indicates. It is also possible that what is meant is that this kind of clothing which was forbidden to them in the world is lawful for them in the Hereafter, and that it is among what they wear there. Thus, in it is what the souls desire, and each one of them is given what his soul desires and attains what he wishes.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 22, verse 17–24 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And they were guided to the good word﴾, i.e., they were guided to it. It has been said it is "There is no god but Allah." It has been said: "Praise be to Allah." It has been said: the Qur'an. It has been said: it is what comes to them from Allah, glorified is He, of good tidings. The Qur'an has indicated what supports this general statement here, namely His saying, glorified is He: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us﴾ [al-Zumar: 74]; ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has guided us to this﴾ [al-A'raf: 43]; ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has removed from us grief﴾ [Fatir: 34]. The meaning of ﴿and they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy﴾ is that they were guided to the praiseworthy path, which is the way to Paradise, or the path of Allah, which is His upright religion, namely Islam.

Thus they are two parties in dispute. This was said by al-Farra' and others. It has been said: the intended meaning of the two adversaries is the Garden and the Fire. The Garden said: "He created me for His mercy," and the Fire said: "He created me for His punishment." It has been said: the intended meaning of the two adversaries is those who came forth on the Day of Badr: from the believers, Hamzah, Ali and Ubaydah; and from the disbelievers, Utbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabi'ah, and al-Walid ibn Utbah. Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, used to swear that this verse was revealed concerning these challengers, as is established from him in the Sahih, and a group of the Companions said the like of this, and they know the causes of revelation better than others. It is also established in the Sahih from Ali that he said: "It was concerning us that this verse was revealed." Ibn Kathir read "Hadhani" (هَذانِّ) with a doubled nun, and He, glorified is He, said "they disputed" (ikhtasamu) and did not say "ikhtasama" (the dual). Al-Farra' said: because they are a plural group; had He said "ikhtasama" it would have been permissible. The meaning of "in their Lord" (fi rabbihim) is: in the matter of their Lord, that is, in His religion, or in His essence, or in His attributes, or in His legislation for His servants, or in all of that. Then He, glorified is He, explained what He had summarized in His saying ﴿He will judge between them﴾, and said: ﴿As for those who disbelieved, garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾. Al-Azhari said: that is, they will be prepared and made into a garment for them. The fire was likened to garments, because it envelops them as garments envelop. He expressed the future by the past to indicate the certainty of its occurrence. It has been said: these garments are of brass that has been melted so that it becomes like fire, and they are the "sarabil" (garments) mentioned in another verse. It has been said: the meaning in the verse is: the fire has encompassed them. It was read "qutti'at" (قُطِعَتْ) with lightening (qutti'at, not qutti'at). Then He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Boiling water will be poured over their heads﴾. The ḥamīm is hot water boiled by the fire of Jahannam, and the clause is either resumptive or is a second predicate of the relative pronoun.

﴿By which that which is in their bellies will be melted﴾. Al-ṣahr is melting, and al-ṣuhāra is what has melted from it. It is said: "ṣahartu al-shay'a fanṣahara," meaning: I melted the thing and it melted, so it is ṣahīr. The meaning is that by that boiling water will be melted what is in their bellies of intestines, viscera and skins. "Skins" is coordinated with "mā": meaning, and the skins will be melted by it. The clause is in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). It has been said: the skins are not melted but burned, so a verb suitable to that is estimated, and it is said: "and the skins will be burned by it," as in the saying of the poet: "I fed her straw and cold water," meaning: and I gave her water to drink. It is not hidden that there is no need for this, for if the ḥamīm melts what is in the bellies, then its melting of the outer skin is more fitting.

﴿And for them are maqāmi' of iron﴾. The maqāmi' is the plural of maqma'ah, and maq'ma'a: I struck him with the miqma'ah, which is a piece of iron. The meaning: for them are maqāmi' of iron with which they will be struck, that is, the disbelievers. The maqāmi' were named maqāmi' because they subdue the one struck, that is, they humiliate him. Ibn al-Sikkit said: "aqma'tu al-rajula 'anni iqma'an" means: when he came upon you and you turned him back from you.

﴿Whenever they wish to come out from it﴾, that is, from the Fire, they will be returned into it, that is, into the Fire, by striking with the maqāmi'. "From grief" (min ghammin) is a substitute for the pronoun in "minha" by repeating the preposition, or it is an object of purpose: meaning, because of a severe grief from the griefs of the Fire. ﴿And taste the punishment of the burning﴾: it is by estimating a saying: that is, they will be returned into it, and it was said: it is said to them: taste the punishment of the burning, that is, the burning punishment. The original meaning of al-ḥarīq is the noun of burning; one burns a thing with fire, and it burns, a burning, and a combustion. Dhawq (tasting) is a contact by which the perception of taste is attained, and it is used here figuratively, and what is meant by it is the perception of pain. Al-Zajjaj said: this is for one of the two adversaries, and he said of the other adversary, who are the believers:

﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who believed and did righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. Thus He, glorified is He, explained the state of the believers after His explanation of the state of the disbelievers. Then Allah, glorified is He, explained some of what He has prepared for them of bliss after their entry into the Garden, and said: ﴿They will be adorned therein﴾. The majority read "yuḥallawna" (يُحَلَّونَ) with doubling and the passive voice, and it was read without doubling: meaning, Allah or the angels by His command will adorn them. "Min" in His saying "min asāwira" (مِن أساوِرَ) is partitive: meaning, they will be adorned with some bracelets; or explanatory; or superfluous. "Min" in "min dhahabin" (مِن ذَهَبٍ) is explanatory. The asāwir are the plural of uswah, and uswah is the plural of siwār, and for siwār there are two dialects: with kasr of the sīn and with ḍamm of it, and there is a third dialect, which is asār. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Asim and Shaybah read "wa-lu'lu'an" (ولُؤْلُؤًا) with the accusative, coordinated with the position of "asāwira": meaning, and they will be adorned with pearls; or by an estimated verb governing its accusative. Likewise Ya'qub, al-Ju'dari and Isa ibn Umar read it with the accusative, and this reading is the one that agrees with the orthography of the Mushaf, since this word is written in it with an alif. The rest read it in the genitive, coordinated with "asāwira": meaning, they will be adorned with bracelets of gold and of pearls. It is not far-fetched that in the Garden there is a bracelet of solid pearl, just as there are bracelets of gold in it.

﴿And their clothing therein is silk﴾: meaning, all that they wear is silk, as this idāfah (construction) indicates. It is also possible that what is meant is that this kind of clothing which was forbidden to them in the world is lawful for them in the Hereafter, and that it is among what they wear there. Thus, in it is what the souls desire, and each one of them is given what his soul desires and attains what he wishes.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 22, verse 17–24 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And they were guided to the good word﴾, i.e., they were guided to it. It has been said it is "There is no god but Allah." It has been said: "Praise be to Allah." It has been said: the Qur'an. It has been said: it is what comes to them from Allah, glorified is He, of good tidings. The Qur'an has indicated what supports this general statement here, namely His saying, glorified is He: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us﴾ [al-Zumar: 74]; ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has guided us to this﴾ [al-A'raf: 43]; ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has removed from us grief﴾ [Fatir: 34]. The meaning of ﴿and they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy﴾ is that they were guided to the praiseworthy path, which is the way to Paradise, or the path of Allah, which is His upright religion, namely Islam.

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿and the Sabians﴾, that he said: they are a people who worship the angels, pray towards the qiblah, and recite the Zabur. ﴿And the Magians﴾ are worshippers of the sun, the moon and the fires. ﴿And those who associated partners﴾ are worshippers of idols. ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them﴾: he said, "The religions are six: five belong to Satan, and the religion of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is one."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Ikrimah regarding the verse that he said: "He decided His judgment between them, so He made the five shared, and made this nation one."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Those who were Jews: the Jews. The Sabians: they have no book. The Magians: the people of idols. And the polytheists: the Christians of the Arabs."

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Abu Dharr that he used to swear an oath that this verse ﴿These two adversaries dispute﴾ up to the end of the verse was revealed concerning the three and the three who fought at the Battle of Badr: Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, 'Ubaydah ibn al-Harith, and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib on one side, and 'Utbah and Shaybah, the sons of Rabi'ah, and al-Walid ibn 'Utbah on the other. 'Ali said: "I will be the first to kneel in dispute before Allah on the Day of Resurrection." al-Bukhari and others related it from the hadith of 'Ali. Ibn Mardawayh related it from Ibn 'Abbas with similar wording, and it has been related likewise from a group of the Followers.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding His saying ﴿Garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾, that he said: "of brass; and there is nothing among vessels that, when heated, is more intensely hot than it." Regarding His saying ﴿Boiling water will be poured over their heads﴾, he said: "the brass will be melted over their heads." His saying ﴿By which what is in their bellies will be melted, and the skins﴾, he said: "their intestines will flow out," and "the skins" – he said: "their skins will be stripped off."

'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sahih, 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Zuhd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who graded it sahih, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Hurayrah that he recited this verse ﴿Boiling water will be poured over their heads﴾ and said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Indeed the boiling water will be poured over their heads, and it will penetrate the skull until it reaches the inside, and it will melt what is in the belly until it passes out through the feet, and that is the melting (al-sahr), and then it will be restored as it was."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿By which what is in their bellies will be melted﴾, that he said: "They walk while their intestines are falling out and their skins."

And regarding His saying ﴿And for them are maqami' of iron﴾, he said: "They will be struck with them, so that each limb falls in its place, and they will call out for destruction and ruin." Ibn Jarir related from him regarding the verse that he said: "They will be given water which, when it enters their bellies, melts them, and the skins along with the bellies."

Ahmad, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who graded it sahih, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th wal-Nushur related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "If a maqma' of iron were placed in the earth and all of mankind and jinn gathered to lift it, they would not be able to lift it from the earth; and if a mountain were struck with a maqma' of iron, it would be shattered and then return as it was."

Ibn al-Mubarak, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Hannad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who graded it sahih, related from Salman, who said: "The Fire is black and dark; its flame does not give light, nor its embers." Then he recited: ﴿Every time they wish to come out of it, out of distress, they will be returned into it﴾.

In the Two Sahihs and others, from 'Umar, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever wears silk in this world will not wear it in the Hereafter." There are other hadiths on this subject.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And they were guided to the good word﴾, that he said: "They were inspired." Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-'Aliyah, who said: "They were guided to the good word in disputing when they said: 'Allah is our Protector, and you have no protector.'" Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid regarding the verse that he said: "The Qur'an." ﴿And they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy﴾: "Islam." Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi (p-960) Hatim related from al-Dahhak regarding the verse that he said: "Islam." Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Zayd, who said: "There is no god but Allah, Allah is greatest, and all praise is due to Allah, who said: ﴿To Him ascends the good word﴾ [Fatir: 10]."

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on surah 22, verses 25–29 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the way of Allah﴾, conjoins the imperfect (*al-mudari‘*, الْمُضَارِعَ) to the perfect (*al-madi*, الْمَاضِيَ), because what is meant by the imperfect is what has already occurred of barring. A similar example is His saying, ﴿Those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the way of Allah﴾ [Muhammad: 1; an-Nahl: 88]. Alternatively, what is meant by barring here is continuity, not merely the future, so the conjunction with the perfect is valid. It is also permissible for the *waw* in *wa-yasudduna* (وَيَصُدُّونَ) to be the *waw* of circumstance, meaning: they disbelieve while they are [in the state of] barring. It has been said that the *waw* is superfluous and the imperfect is the predicate of *inna* (إِنَّ). The better view is that the predicate of *inna* is to be understood after His saying, "and the desert-dweller" (وَالْبَادِ), and it is like [the omitted predicate in the sense of] "they have lost" or "they have perished." Al-Zajjaj said that the predicate of *inna* is ﴿and We will make him taste of a painful punishment﴾. This was refuted on the grounds that if it were the predicate of *inna*, the verb would not be in the jussive, and also that if it were the predicate of *inna*, the conditional clause would remain without an answer [since the conditional *man* in "wa-man yurid" would lack its response]. The better view is that it is omitted, as we have mentioned.

What is meant by *al-saddu* (الصَّدُّ, barring) is prevention, and "the way of Allah" is His religion. That is: they prevent those who wish to enter the religion of Allah and the Sacred Mosque. It is conjoined to "the way of Allah." It has been said that what is meant is the Mosque itself, as is apparent from this Qur'anic wording. It has also been said that it refers to the whole Sacred Precinct (*al-haram*, الْحَرَمُ), because the polytheists barred the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions on the day of al-Hudaybiyyah. It has been said that what is meant is Makkah, by the evidence of His saying, ﴿which We made for the people [as a place] of equal [right], the one residing therein and the visitor﴾. That is: We made it for the people in general, they pray in it and circumambulate it, and the one residing in it (*al-‘akif*, الْعَاكِفُ), that is, the one who stays and remains there, and the desert-dweller (*al-badi*, الْبَادِي), that is, the one who arrives from the desert, and what is meant by him is the one who comes to it from outside, without distinction between whether he is from the people of the desert or from others. The accusative of *sawa’* (سَوَاءً) is that it is the second object of *ja‘alnahu* (جَعَلْنَاهُ), and it has the sense of "equal" (*mustawiyan*, مُسْتَوِيًا), and *al-‘akif* is raised by it. The Sacred Mosque was described thus in order to add to the rebuke and reproach of those who bar [others] from it. It is possible that the accusative of *sawa’* is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*, حَالٌ).

This is according to the reading with the accusative, and Hafs transmitted it from ‘Asim, and it is the recitation (*qira’a*, قِرَاءَةٌ, a canonical mode of reciting the Qur'an) of al-A‘mash. The majority read *sawa’un* (سَوَاءٌ) with *raf‘* (nominative), as the subject with *al-‘akif* as its predicate, or as a preposed predicate with *al-‘akif* as the subject, meaning: *al-‘akif fihi* (the one residing in it) and *al-badi* are equal. It has also been read with *sawa’an* in the accusative and *al-‘akifi* (الْعَاكِفِ) in the genitive, as an adjective of "the people," meaning: We made it for the people, [in which] the one residing and the visitor are equal. Ibn Kathir pronounced the *ya’* in *al-badi* (الْبَادِي) both in continuous recitation and in pause, while Abu ‘Amr omitted it in pause, and Nafi‘ omitted it both in continuous recitation and in pause.

Al-Qurtubi said: The people have unanimously agreed on equality concerning the Sacred Mosque itself. They differed concerning Makkah. Mujahid and Malik held that the houses and dwellings of Makkah are equal, in that the resident and the newcomer share them alike. ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn ‘Abbas and a group held that the newcomer may lodge wherever he finds a place, and the owner of the dwelling must give him shelter, whether he wishes or not. The majority held that the houses and dwellings of Makkah are not like the Sacred Mosque, and its residents have the right to prevent the newcomer from lodging in them. The summary is that the discussion of this matter returns to two principles. The first principle concerns what is in this verse: is what is meant by the Sacred Mosque the mosque itself, or the whole Sacred Precinct, or Makkah in particular? The second concerns whether the conquest of Makkah was by treaty or by force. And if we assume it was by force, did the Prophet (ﷺ) leave it in the hands of its inhabitants in particular, or did he make it open to all who entered it? We have explained this in our commentary on *al-Muntaqa*, in a manner that the reader will not need anything further.

﴿And whoever intends therein deviation with wrong-doing, We will make him taste of a painful punishment﴾. The object of *yurid* (يُرِدْ) is omitted for the purpose of generality, and the estimate is: "whoever intends therein an intention," that is, an intention of deviation (*ilhad*, إِلْحَادٍ), that is, of departing from the aim. *Al-ilhad* in the language means inclination, except that He, glorified is He, clarified here that it is inclination with wrong-doing. The scholars differed about what this wrong-doing is. It has been said that it is polytheism. It has been said: polytheism and killing. It has been said: hunting its animals and cutting its trees. It has been said: swearing oaths therein with false oaths. It has been said: what is meant is sins therein in general. It has been said: what is meant by this verse is that one is punished merely for intending disobedience in that place. Ibn Mas‘ud, Ibn ‘Umar, al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd and others held this view, to the extent that they said: if a man intended in the Sanctuary to kill a man in Aden, Allah would punish him. The summary is that this verse indicates that whoever is in the Sacred House is held accountable merely for the intention to do wrong. It therefore specifies the report that Allah forgave this nation what its souls whisper, unless it is said that intention there involves more than mere inner speech. In sum, to investigate this matter and to establish the truth in it in a way that unites the evidences and removes the difficulty would be very lengthy. Similar to this verse is the hadith: "When two Muslims meet with their swords, the killer and the killed are in the Fire." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, this is the killer, but what about the killed?" He said: "He was eager to kill his companion." So he entered the Fire here merely because of his eagerness to kill his companion. We have devoted a separate treatise to this study.

The *ba’* (بِ) in His saying *bi-ilhadin* (بِإِلْحَادٍ): if the object of *yurid* is omitted as we have mentioned, then it is not superfluous. It has been said that it is superfluous here, like the words of the poet:

*We are the sons of Ja‘dah, the owners of al-Falaj;*
*we strike with the sword and hope for relief.*

That is, "we hope for relief." Similar to it is:

*Has news not come to you, while tidings are spread,*
*of what the she-camels of the Banu Ziyad encountered?*

That is, "what they encountered." Among those who said it is superfluous is al-Akhfash, and the meaning according to him is: "whoever intends therein deviation with wrong-doing." The Kufans said: the *ba’* entered because the meaning is "that he deviates" (*bi-an yulhida*, بِأَنْ يُلْحِدَ), and the *ba’* with *an* (أَنْ) may enter and may be omitted. It is also permissible that the estimate is: "whoever intends people with deviation."

It has been said: *yurid* is implicitly including the meaning of *yahumm* (يَهُمُّ, to resolve), and the meaning is: "whoever resolves therein upon deviation."

As for the *ba’* in His saying *bi-zulmin* (بِظُلْمٍ), it denotes cause (*sababiyya*, سَبَبِيَّةٌ), and the meaning is: "whoever intends therein deviation because of wrong-doing." It is also permissible that *bi-zulmin* is a substitute (*badal*, بَدَلٌ) for *bi-ilhadin*, with the preposition repeated, and it is also permissible that both are two synonymous circumstantial clauses.

﴿And [mention] when We settled for Ibrahim the site of the House﴾. That is: and remember the time of that. It is said *bawwa’tuhu manzilan* (بَوَّأْتُهُ مَنْزِلًا, I settled him in a dwelling) and *bawwa’tu lahu* (بَوَّأْتُ لَهُ), just as one says *makkantuka* (مَكَّنْتُكَ) and *makkantu laka* (مَكَّنْتُ لَكَ).

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: We made the site of the House a place settled (*mubawwa’*, مُبَوَّأً) for Ibrahim. The meaning of *bawwa’na* (بَوَّأْنَا) is: We showed him the site of the House. A similar usage is the words of the poet:

*How many a noble brother of mine did I lay down with my own hands in a grave.*

Al-Farra’ said: the *lam* is superfluous, and *makan* (مَكَانَ) is an adverb of place, meaning: We caused him to dwell in it.

﴿that you not associate anything with Me﴾. It has been said that this is explanatory (*mufassira*, مُفَسِّرَةٌ) of *bawwa’na*, because it includes the sense of *ta‘abbadna* (تَعَبَّدْنَا, We made you worship), since settling was for worship. Abu Hatim said it is verbal-masdar (*masdariyya*, مَصْدَرِيَّةٌ), meaning: "so that you do not associate." It has been said that it is the lightened form of the heavy one (*al-mukhaffafa min al-thaqila*, الْمُخَفَّفَةُ مِنَ الثَّقِيلَةِ), and it has been said that it is superfluous. It has also been said that the meaning of the verse is: "We revealed to him that you should not worship other than Me."

Al-Mubarrad said: it is as if it were said to him: "Make Me one [God] in this house," because the meaning of *la tushrik bi* (لاَ تُشْرِكْ بِي, do not associate with Me) is: "Make Me One."

﴿and purify My House﴾ from polytheism and the worship of idols. In the verse there is a criticism of those of the inhabitants of the House who committed polytheism, meaning: this was the condition upon your forefather, and then whoever came after him, and you did not fulfill it, but rather you associated [others with Allah].

One group said that the address in His saying *an la tushrik* is to Muhammad (ﷺ), but this is very weak.

The meaning of ﴿and purify My House﴾ is purifying it from disbelief, idols, blood and all other impurities. It has been said that it refers only to purifying it from idols, because the Jurhum and the 'Amaliq had idols in the place of the House. What is sufficient for this meaning has passed in the surah of Bara’ah. What is meant by *al-qa’imin* (الْقَائِمِينَ, those who stand) here are those who pray. The mention of ﴿those who bow and prostrate﴾ after it is to explain the pillars of prayer, as an indication of the greatness of this act of worship. He joined circumambulation with prayer, because both are prescribed only in the House; so the circumambulation is at it and the prayer is toward it.

﴿And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage﴾. Al-Hasan and Ibn Muhaysin read *wa-adhin* (وَآذِنْ), with the *dhal* lightened and with the long vowel. The rest read it with the *dhal* doubled. *Al-adhan* (الأَذَانُ) means announcement (*al-i‘lam*, الإِعْلَامُ), and it has been discussed earlier in Bara’ah.

Al-Wahidi said: The group of exegetes said: When Ibrahim finished building the House, Jibril came to him and commanded him to proclaim the pilgrimage among the people. He said: "O Lord, who will convey my voice?" Allah, glorified is He, said: "Proclaim, and upon Me is the delivery." So he ascended the station (*al-maqam*, الْمَقَامَ) and rose with it until it became like the highest mountains. He put his two fingers into his ears, turned his face right and left, east and west, and said: "O people, the pilgrimage to the House has been prescribed for you, so answer your Lord." So those who were in the loins of men and the wombs of women answered him: "Here I am, O Allah, here I am."

It has been said that the address is to our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). The meaning is: inform them, O Muhammad, of the obligation of the pilgrimage upon them. According to this, the address is to Ibrahim up to His saying, ﴿those who bow and prostrate﴾. It has been said that his address ends at His saying, ﴿And [mention] when We settled for Ibrahim the site of the House﴾, and that His saying, ﴿that you not associate anything with Me﴾ and what follows it is an address to our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ).

The majority read *al-hajj* (الْحَجِّ) with a *fatha* on the *ha’*. Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with a *kasra* throughout the Qur'an.

﴿They will come to you on foot﴾. This is the answer to the command. Allah promised that the people's response to His call to the pilgrimage to the House would be on foot and on mounts. The meaning of *rijalan* (رِجَالًا) is walking, and it is the plural of *rajil* (رَاجِل, walker). It has been said that it is the plural of *rajul* (رَجُل, man).

Ibn Abi Ishaq read *rujalan* (رُجَالًا) with a *damma* on the *ra’* and a lightened *jim*. Mujahid read *rujala* (رُجَالَى) on the pattern of *fu‘ala*, like *kusala* (كُسَالَى, lazy). He put *al-rijal* before *al-rukban* (the riders) in mention because of the increase in their hardship in walking. He said *ya’tuka* (يَأْتُوكَ, they will come to you), although they come to the House, because whoever came to the Ka‘bah as a pilgrim has come to Ibrahim, because he answered his call.

﴿and on every lean camel﴾. It is conjoined to *rijalan*, meaning: and riders on every camel. The *dhamir* (ضَامِرٌ, lean) is a camel that is emaciated and whom the journey has exhausted. One says *damura yadmuru dumuran* (ضَمُرَ يَضْمُرُ ضُمُورًا). He described *al-dhamir* with *ya’tina* (يَأْتِينَ, they come, feminine plural) with regard to meaning, because *al-dhamir* has the sense of *dhawamir* (ضَوَامِرَ, lean ones). The companions of Ibn Mas‘ud, Ibn Abi ‘Abla and al-Dahhak read *ya’tuna* (يَأْتُونَ) as an adjective of *rijalan*.

*Al-fajj* (الْفَجُّ) is the wide road, its plural is *fijaj* (فِجَاجٌ), and *al-‘amiq* (الْعَمِيقُ) is the distant.

The *lam* in ﴿that they may witness benefits for them﴾ is connected to His saying *ya’tuka* (يَأْتُوكَ). It has been said it is connected to His saying *wa-adhin*. *Al-shuhud* (الشُّهُودُ) is presence, and *al-manafi‘* (الْمَنَافِعُ, the benefits) includes the benefits of this world and the Hereafter. It has been said that what is meant by it is the rites (*al-manasik*, الْمَنَاسِكُ). It has been said: forgiveness. It has been said: trade, as in His saying, ﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198].

﴿and mention the name of Allah on known days﴾, that is, they mention the name of Allah at the slaughter of the offerings and sacrificial animals. It has been said that this mention is an allusion to slaughter, because it is inseparable from it.

The known days are the days of sacrifice (*ayyam al-nahr*), as His saying indicates: ﴿over what He has provided them of the grazing livestock﴾. It has been said: the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah.

The discussion of "the known days" and "the counted days" has already passed in al-Baqarah, so we will not repeat it. The discussion of the time of the slaughter of the sacrifice is well known in the books of jurisprudence and the commentaries on hadith. The meaning of ﴿over what He has provided them﴾ is: over the slaughter of what He has provided them of the grazing livestock, which are camels, cattle and sheep. The grazing livestock (*bahimat al-an‘am*, بَهِيمَةُ الأَنْعَامِ) is the same as *al-an‘am*, so the genitive construction here is like the construction in their saying *masjid al-jami‘* (مَسْجِدُ الْجَامِعِ) and *salat al-ula* (صَلاَةُ الأُولَى).

﴿So eat from them﴾. The imperative here is for recommendation (*al-nadb*, النَّدْبِ) according to the majority. A group held that the imperative is for obligation (*al-wujub*, الْوُجُوبِ). This is a shift (*iltifat*, الْتِفَاتٌ) from the third person to the second person.

﴿and feed the miserable, the poor﴾. *Al-ba’is* (الْبَائِسُ) is one possessed of misery (*al-bu’s*, الْبُؤْسُ), which is extreme poverty. Therefore *al-faqir* (الْفَقِيرَ) is mentioned after it for further clarification. The imperative here is for obligation, and it has been said for recommendation.

﴿Then let them end their state of unkemptness﴾. What is meant by *al-qada’* (الْقَضَاءُ) here is performance (*al-ta’diya*, التَّأْدِيَةُ), that is: let them perform the removal of their filth, because *al-tafath* (التَّفَثُ) is filth and squalor from long hair and nails. The exegetes, as al-Naysaburi related, have unanimously agreed on this.

Al-Zajjaj said: the people of the language do not know *al-tafath*.

Abu ‘Ubayda said: nothing has come in poetry that can be cited as evidence for the meaning of *al-tafath*.

Al-Mubarrad said: The original meaning of tafath (dirt, untidiness) in the language is every filth that clings to a person.

It was also said: "Its fulfilment (qada') is his grooming (idhhan)," because the pilgrim is dusty and unkempt, not having applied oil or removed hair; so when he completes his rites and comes out of his state of ihram, he shaves his head and wears his clothes. This is the fulfilment of tafath.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is as if it were an exit from ihram into the permitted state. ﴿And let them fulfil their vows﴾ — that is, what they vow of righteousness during their pilgrimage. The command is one of obligation. It was also said that the vows here refer to the acts of the Hajj. ﴿And let them circumambulate the Ancient House﴾ (p-962): this circumambulation is the Tawaf al-Ifadah.

Ibn Jarir said: There is no disagreement among the interpreters on this. "Ancient" (ʿatiq) means old, as His words, glorified be He, indicate: ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind﴾ [Al 'Imran: 96], and so on. It was named ʿatiq because God freed it (aʿtaqahu) from being dominated by any tyrant. It was also said: because God frees the necks of sinners from punishment within it. It was also said: because it was freed from the flood's drowning. And it was said: ʿatiq means noble.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿and the Sacred Mosque﴾ that he said: "The whole Haram, and it is the Sacred Mosque." ﴿equal for the one who resides therein and the one who comes from outside﴾: he said, "God's creation in it is equal." Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr the like of it.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse that he said: "They are equal in the dwellings of Mecca, so the people of Mecca should make room for them until they complete their rites."

Al-Badi and the people of Mecca are equal, meaning in the dwelling and the Haram.

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr who said: "Whoever takes rent from the houses of Mecca, he is only eating fire into his belly."

Ibn Saʿd narrated from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab that a man said to him at al-Marwah: "O Commander of the Faithful, grant me a plot of land for myself and my descendants." ʿUmar turned away from him and said: "It is the Sanctuary of God; the resident and the visitor are equal in it."

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from ʿAta who said: "ʿUmar used to prevent the people of Mecca from making doors for their houses, until the pilgrim could alight in the courtyards of the houses."

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated, al-Suyuti said with a sound chain, from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said, concerning God's words, "﴿equal for the one who resides therein and the one who comes from outside﴾": "Equal are the resident and the one who enters."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Mecca is open to all; its houses are not to be rented out and its plots are not to be sold."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Majah narrated from ʿAlqamah ibn Nadlah who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) died, and Abu Bakr and ʿUmar too, and the plots of Mecca were called only 'al-sawaʾib' (free to all): whoever needed would dwell, and whoever was rich would let others dwell."

Ibn Majah narrated it from Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah, from ʿIsa ibn Yunus, from ʿUmar ibn Saʿid ibn Abi Hafrah, from ʿUthman ibn Abi Sulayman, from ʿAlqamah, and so he mentioned it.

Al-Daraqutni narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever eats the rent of the houses of Mecca, eats fire."

Al-Firyabi, Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn Rahawayh, Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Bazzar, Abu Yaʿla, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Masʿud, traced to the Prophet, concerning His words ﴿and whoever wills therein deviation by wrongdoing﴾: "If a man intended therein deviation while he was in Aden-Abyan, God would make him taste a painful punishment."

Ibn Kathir said: This chain is sound according to the conditions of al-Bukhari, but its being a statement of Ibn Masʿud (mawquf) is more fitting than its being traced to the Prophet, and for this reason Shu'bah insisted on its being halted.

Saʿid ibn Mansur and al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn Masʿud concerning the verse that he said: "Whoever intends a sin, but does not do it outside the House, it is not recorded against him until he does it; and whoever intends a sin within the House, God will not cause him to die in this world until He makes him taste a painful punishment."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: This verse was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allah ibn Unays: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent him with two men, one of them a Muhajir and the other an Ansari. They boasted about lineages, so ʿAbd Allah ibn Unays became angry, killed the Ansari, then apostatized from Islam and fled to Mecca, and this verse was revealed about him: ﴿and whoever wills therein deviation by wrongdoing﴾, meaning whoever seeks refuge in the Haram with deviation, meaning inclination away from Islam.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning the words ﴿and whoever wills therein deviation by wrongdoing﴾ that he said: "It means associating partners (with God)."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari in his History, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Yaʿla ibn Umayyah, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: "Hoarding food in the Haram is deviation therein."

Saʿid ibn Mansur, al-Bukhari in his History and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab who said: "Hoarding food in Mecca is deviation by wrongdoing."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿUmar who said: "Selling food in Mecca is deviation."

Al-Bayhaqi in Shuʿab al-Iman narrated from him who said: "I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: 'Hoarding food in Mecca is deviation.'"

Ibn Jarir and al-Hakim (who graded it sound) narrated from ʿAli who said: "When Ibrahim was commanded to build the House, Isma'il and Hajar went out with him, and that was when God says: ﴿And when We settled for Ibrahim the place of the House﴾, and so on."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from ʿAta concerning ﴿and those who stand﴾ that he said: "Those who pray beside it."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah the same meaning.

Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf, Ibn Mani', Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound) and al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "When Ibrahim finished building the House, he said: 'My Lord, I have finished.' He said: ﴿And proclaim to the people the Hajj﴾. He said: 'My Lord, what will my voice reach?' He said: 'Proclaim, and upon Me is the delivery.' He said: 'My Lord, how shall I say it?' He said: 'Say: O people, the Hajj to the Ancient House has been prescribed for you.' So whoever is in the heavens and the earth heard it. Do you not see that they come from the farthest parts of the earth, reciting the talbiyah?" On this subject there are reports from a group of the Companions.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿that they may witness benefits for themselves﴾ that he said: "Markets that were theirs; God mentions only worldly benefits."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him who said: "Benefits in this world and benefits in the Hereafter. As for the benefits of the Hereafter, they are God's pleasure; and as for the benefits of this world, they are what they obtain of the flesh of the camels on that day, and of the sacrifices, and of trade."

Abu Bakr al-Marwazi in Kitab al-ʿIdayn narrated from him, also, who said: "The known days: the Day of Sacrifice and three days after it."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him, also, who said: "The known days: the Day of Sacrifice and three days after it."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him, also, who said: "The Days of Tashriq."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him, also, concerning the known days, that he said: "The day before the Day of Tarwiyah, and the Day of Tarwiyah and the Day of ʿArafah."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him, also, who said: "Al-ba'is is the disabled (zamin)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿUmar (p-963) who said: "Al-tafath is all the rites."

These same narrators reported similarly from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Saʿid ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "Al-tafath is shaving the head, trimming the sideburns, plucking the armpit hair, shaving the pubic area, standing at ʿArafah, running between al-Safa and al-Marwah, stoning the Jamarat, cutting the nails, trimming the moustache, and slaughtering."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him concerning ﴿and let them circumambulate the Ancient House﴾ that it is the Tawaf al-Ziyarah on the Day of Sacrifice. Reports on the reason the House is called "ancient" have been transmitted from a group of the Companions, and we have already pointed to that earlier. Hadiths on the virtue of circumambulation have also been transmitted, but this is not the place to mention them.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on surah 22, verses 25–29 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the way of Allah﴾, conjoins the imperfect (*al-mudari‘*, الْمُضَارِعَ) to the perfect (*al-madi*, الْمَاضِيَ), because what is meant by the imperfect is what has already occurred of barring. A similar example is His saying, ﴿Those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the way of Allah﴾ [Muhammad: 1; an-Nahl: 88]. Alternatively, what is meant by barring here is continuity, not merely the future, so the conjunction with the perfect is valid. It is also permissible for the *waw* in *wa-yasudduna* (وَيَصُدُّونَ) to be the *waw* of circumstance, meaning: they disbelieve while they are [in the state of] barring. It has been said that the *waw* is superfluous and the imperfect is the predicate of *inna* (إِنَّ). The better view is that the predicate of *inna* is to be understood after His saying, "and the desert-dweller" (وَالْبَادِ), and it is like [the omitted predicate in the sense of] "they have lost" or "they have perished." Al-Zajjaj said that the predicate of *inna* is ﴿and We will make him taste of a painful punishment﴾. This was refuted on the grounds that if it were the predicate of *inna*, the verb would not be in the jussive, and also that if it were the predicate of *inna*, the conditional clause would remain without an answer [since the conditional *man* in "wa-man yurid" would lack its response]. The better view is that it is omitted, as we have mentioned.

What is meant by *al-saddu* (الصَّدُّ, barring) is prevention, and "the way of Allah" is His religion. That is: they prevent those who wish to enter the religion of Allah and the Sacred Mosque. It is conjoined to "the way of Allah." It has been said that what is meant is the Mosque itself, as is apparent from this Qur'anic wording. It has also been said that it refers to the whole Sacred Precinct (*al-haram*, الْحَرَمُ), because the polytheists barred the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions on the day of al-Hudaybiyyah. It has been said that what is meant is Makkah, by the evidence of His saying, ﴿which We made for the people [as a place] of equal [right], the one residing therein and the visitor﴾. That is: We made it for the people in general, they pray in it and circumambulate it, and the one residing in it (*al-‘akif*, الْعَاكِفُ), that is, the one who stays and remains there, and the desert-dweller (*al-badi*, الْبَادِي), that is, the one who arrives from the desert, and what is meant by him is the one who comes to it from outside, without distinction between whether he is from the people of the desert or from others. The accusative of *sawa’* (سَوَاءً) is that it is the second object of *ja‘alnahu* (جَعَلْنَاهُ), and it has the sense of "equal" (*mustawiyan*, مُسْتَوِيًا), and *al-‘akif* is raised by it. The Sacred Mosque was described thus in order to add to the rebuke and reproach of those who bar [others] from it. It is possible that the accusative of *sawa’* is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*, حَالٌ).

This is according to the reading with the accusative, and Hafs transmitted it from ‘Asim, and it is the recitation (*qira’a*, قِرَاءَةٌ, a canonical mode of reciting the Qur'an) of al-A‘mash. The majority read *sawa’un* (سَوَاءٌ) with *raf‘* (nominative), as the subject with *al-‘akif* as its predicate, or as a preposed predicate with *al-‘akif* as the subject, meaning: *al-‘akif fihi* (the one residing in it) and *al-badi* are equal. It has also been read with *sawa’an* in the accusative and *al-‘akifi* (الْعَاكِفِ) in the genitive, as an adjective of "the people," meaning: We made it for the people, [in which] the one residing and the visitor are equal. Ibn Kathir pronounced the *ya’* in *al-badi* (الْبَادِي) both in continuous recitation and in pause, while Abu ‘Amr omitted it in pause, and Nafi‘ omitted it both in continuous recitation and in pause.

Al-Qurtubi said: The people have unanimously agreed on equality concerning the Sacred Mosque itself. They differed concerning Makkah. Mujahid and Malik held that the houses and dwellings of Makkah are equal, in that the resident and the newcomer share them alike. ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn ‘Abbas and a group held that the newcomer may lodge wherever he finds a place, and the owner of the dwelling must give him shelter, whether he wishes or not. The majority held that the houses and dwellings of Makkah are not like the Sacred Mosque, and its residents have the right to prevent the newcomer from lodging in them. The summary is that the discussion of this matter returns to two principles. The first principle concerns what is in this verse: is what is meant by the Sacred Mosque the mosque itself, or the whole Sacred Precinct, or Makkah in particular? The second concerns whether the conquest of Makkah was by treaty or by force. And if we assume it was by force, did the Prophet (ﷺ) leave it in the hands of its inhabitants in particular, or did he make it open to all who entered it? We have explained this in our commentary on *al-Muntaqa*, in a manner that the reader will not need anything further.

﴿And whoever intends therein deviation with wrong-doing, We will make him taste of a painful punishment﴾.
