The sentence ﴿وَمَنْ يُشْرِكْ بِاللَّهِ فَكَأَنَّمَا خَرَّ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ﴾ (and whoever associates others with Allah is as if he had fallen from the sky) is a new sentence that emphasizes what came before it of the command to avoid. The meaning of "fell from the sky" is: he fell to the earth, that is, he dropped from the lofty height of faith to the abyss of disbelief. ﴿فَتَخْطَفُهُ الطَّيْرُ﴾ (then the birds snatch him): one says khaṭafahu yakhṭifuhu when he seizes it, and from the same root is His statement ﴿يَخْطَفُ أَبْصَارَهُمْ﴾ (it nearly snatches away their sight) [al-Baqara 2:20], meaning it tears their flesh and cuts it with its talons.

Abu Ja'far and Nafi' read takhattafu with a shadda on the ṭāʾ and a fatḥa on the khāʾ. It is also read with a kasra on the khāʾ and the ṭāʾ, and with a kasra on the tāʾ as well as on both of those letters. ﴿أَوْ تَهْوِي بِهِ الرِّيحُ﴾ means: or the wind hurls it and throws it down ﴿فِي مَكَانٍ سَحِيقٍ﴾ (into a far-off place), that is, a distant place. One says saḥuqa yasḥuqu saḥqan, so he is saḥīq when he has gone far.

Al-Zajjaj said: Allah has informed us that the distance of one who associates others with Him from the truth is like the distance of one who has fallen from the sky, so the birds carry him off or the wind throws him into a distant place.

﴿ذَلِكَ وَمَنْ يُعَظِّمْ شَعَائِرَ اللَّهِ﴾: the discussion of this demonstrative (dhalika) has been given shortly before. The shaʿāʾir (rites) is the plural of shaʿīrah, which is everything in which there is a sign (shiʿār) for Allah, the Exalted. From the same root is the shiʿār of a people in war, which is their identifying sign by which they recognize each other. From the same root is ish'ār al-budn (marking the sacrificial camels), which is stabbing the right side of the hump. So the shaʿāʾir of Allah are the markers of His religion. The sacrificial animals (hadāyā) enter the rites of Hajj at the primary level.

The pronoun in ﴿فَإِنَّهَا مِنْ تَقْوَى الْقُلُوبِ﴾ (for it is from the piety of hearts) refers to the shaʿāʾir, with an omitted genitive construction, meaning: indeed, glorifying them is from the piety of hearts, that is, from the actions of the hearts which belong to taqwā (God-consciousness). This glorification arises from taqwā.

﴿لَكُمْ فِيهَا مَنَافِعُ﴾ (you have benefits in them) means in the rites in general, or in particular, and in particular means the camels, as the context indicates. Among their benefits are riding, milk, offspring, wool, and other things ﴿إِلَى أَجَلٍ مُسَمًّى﴾ (until an appointed term), which is the time of their slaughter, ﴿ثُمَّ مَحِلُّهَا إِلَى الْبَيْتِ الْعَتِيقِ﴾ (then their place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House), meaning where their slaughter takes place. The meaning is that they reach the House and the Sacred Precinct around it, so their worldly benefits derived from them continue until the time of their slaughter, and after that their benefits become religious.

It has been said that maḥilluhā here is derived from iḥlāl al-ḥarām (making the forbidden lawful, i.e., releasing from iḥram). The meaning is that all the rites of Hajj, from standing at ʿArafa, stoning the pillars (rami al-jimar), and sa'y, end with the ṭawāf al-ifāḍa at the House, so the House is intended in itself according to this view.

﴿وَلِكُلِّ أُمَّةٍ جَعَلْنَا مَنْسَكًا﴾: al-mansak here is a verbal noun from nasaka yansuku, when one slaughters a sacrifice for worship (qurbān). A slaughtered animal is nasīkah, and its plural is nusuk.

Al-Azhari said: the intended meaning of mansak in the verse is the place of sacrifice. It is said mansik and mansak, with kasra and fatḥa on the sīn, two dialects. The Kufans read it with a kasra except ʿĀṣim, and the rest read it with a fatḥa.

Al-Farra' said: in the language of the Arabs, mansak is the customary place for good or evil. Ibn ʿArafa said of ﴿وَلِكُلِّ أُمَّةٍ جَعَلْنَا مَنْسَكًا﴾: meaning a path (madhhab) of obedience to Allah.

It is also narrated from al-Farra' that mansak means the festival (ʿīd). It has been said that it means Hajj. The first view is more fitting because of His statement ﴿لِيَذْكُرُوا اسْمَ اللَّهِ﴾ (so that they may mention the name of Allah) and onward. The ummah is the community united upon one path. The meaning is: We appointed for every people of the religions a slaughter they perform and blood they shed, or a form of worship, or obedience, or a festival, or a Hajj they make pilgrimage to, so that they may mention the name of Allah alone and make their rites exclusively for Him ﴿عَلَى مَا رَزَقَهُمْ مِنْ بَهِيمَةِ الْأَنْعَامِ﴾ (over what He has provided them of the beasts of cattle), meaning over the slaughter of what He has provided them from them. In this is an indication that a sacrifice can only be from the livestock and not from anything else. The verse is evidence that the purpose of the mentioned slaughter is mentioning the name of Allah over it.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, informed them of His singularity in divinity and that He has no partner. The fāʾ is for ordering what follows upon what precedes. Then He commanded them to submit to Him and to yield to His obedience and worship. Placing the prepositional phrase before the verb is for restriction (qaṣr), and the fāʾ here is like the fāʾ before it.

Then He commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to give glad tidings to the mukhbitīn among His servants, meaning the humble, the submissive, the sincere. It is derived from al-khabt, which is low ground. The meaning is: give them glad tidings, O Muhammad, of the abundant reward and great gifts that Allah has prepared for them.

It has been said that the mukhbitīn are those who do not wrong others, and when others wrong them they do not seek retribution.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, described these mukhbitīn with His statement ﴿الَّذِينَ إِذَا ذُكِرَ اللَّهُ وَجِلَتْ قُلُوبُهُمْ﴾ (those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned), meaning they fear and beware of disobeying Him. The occurrence of trembling in them at the mention of Him, glory be to Him, is evidence of the perfection of their certainty and the strength of their faith. He described them with patience ﴿عَلَى مَا أَصَابَهُمْ﴾ (over what befalls them) of afflictions and trials in obedience to Allah. Then He described them with establishing the prayer, meaning performing it at its times in the most complete manner.

The majority read ﴿وَالْمُقِيمِي الصَّلَاةِ﴾ (wal-muqīmī al-ṣalāh) with a kasra, as is apparent. Abu ʿAmr read it with a fatḥa, as if the nūn were still retained (wal-muqīmīna). Sibawayh cited as evidence for that the verse of the poet:

"The guardian of the honour of the tribe..." (the whole line), with the accusative on ʿawrata (ʿawrah, honour/vulnerable point).

It has been said that Abu ʿAmr did not read with this reading. Ibn Muhaysin read wal-muqīmīna with the nūn retained according to the original form, and this reading is narrated from Ibn Masʿūd. Then He described them, glory be to Him, with His statement ﴿وَمِمَّا رَزَقْنَاهُمْ يُنْفِقُونَ﴾ (and from what We have provided them they spend), meaning they give charity from it, spending it in the paths of righteousness and placing it in the places of good. A similar verse is His statement, glory be to Him: ﴿إِنَّمَا الْمُؤْمِنُونَ الَّذِينَ إِذَا ذُكِرَ اللَّهُ وَجِلَتْ قُلُوبُهُمْ وَإِذَا تُلِيَتْ عَلَيْهِمْ آيَاتُهُ زَادَتْهُمْ إِيمَانًا وَعَلَى رَبِّهِمْ يَتَوَكَّلُونَ﴾ (The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, and when His verses are recited to them they increase them in faith, and upon their Lord they rely).

Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding His statement ﴿حُرُمَاتِ اللَّهِ﴾ (the sacred things of Allah): he said, "The sacred things are Makkah, the Hajj and the ʿUmrah, and everything Allah has forbidden of His disobediences, all of them."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His statement ﴿فَاجْتَنِبُوا الرِّجْسَ مِنَ الْأَوْثَانِ﴾: he said, "Avoid obeying Satan in the worship of idols." ﴿وَاجْتَنِبُوا قَوْلَ الزُّورِ﴾: he means slandering Allah and denying Him.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ayman ibn Khuraym, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood up delivering a sermon and said: "O people, false testimony has been made equal to associating partners with Allah," three times. Then he recited ﴿فَاجْتَنِبُوا الرِّجْسَ مِنَ الْأَوْثَانِ وَاجْتَنِبُوا قَوْلَ الزُّورِ﴾.

Ahmad said: it is gharīb (a strange narration); we know it only from the narration of Sufyan ibn Zayd. It has been differently reported from him in narrating this hadith, and we do not know of Ayman ibn Khuraym having heard from the Prophet (ﷺ).

It was also narrated by Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab, from the hadith of Khuraym.

It is firmly established in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs and others, from the hadith of Abu Bakra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Shall I not inform you of the greatest of the major sins?" three times. We said, "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said, "Associating partners with Allah, and disobedience to parents." He had been reclining, so he sat up and said, "Beware, and the word of falsehood. Beware, and false testimony." He kept repeating it until we said, "I wish he would stop."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His statement ﴿حُنَفَاءَ لِلَّهِ غَيْرَ مُشْرِكِينَ بِهِ﴾: he said, "Pilgrims to Allah, not associating anything with Him." This is because the people of jāhiliyyah used to make the pilgrimage while associating partners, but when Allah made Islam manifest, Allah said to the Muslims: "Make the pilgrimage now, not associating anything with Allah."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His statement ﴿وَمَنْ يُعَظِّمْ شَعَائِرَ اللَّهِ﴾: he said, "The budn (sacrificial camels)."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿وَمَنْ يُعَظِّمْ شَعَائِرَ اللَّهِ﴾: he said, "Choosing the fattest, the finest, and the most magnificent." And regarding His statement ﴿لَكُمْ فِيهَا مَنَافِعُ إِلَى أَجَلٍ مُسَمًّى﴾: he said, "Until they are named budn."

These same narrators also narrated similarly from Mujahid, and in it he said: "﴿لَكُمْ فِيهَا مَنَافِعُ إِلَى أَجَلٍ مُسَمًّى﴾: in their backs, their milk, their wool, their hair and their fleece, until they are named hady (sacrificial offering). When they are named hady, the benefits go away. Then ﴿مَحِلُّهَا﴾ (their place) — he says: when they are named — ﴿إِلَى الْبَيْتِ الْعَتِيقِ﴾."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʿIkrima, who said: "When it enters the Sacred Precinct, it has reached its place."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His statement ﴿وَلِكُلِّ أُمَّةٍ جَعَلْنَا مَنْسَكًا﴾: he said, "A festival."

Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding the verse: he said, "The shedding of blood."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from ʿIkrima, who said: "Slaughter."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam regarding the verse, who said: "Makkah. Allah has not appointed any community a mansak other than it."

Hadiths about the sacrifice (udhiyya) have been reported, but this is not the place to mention them.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding His statement ﴿وَبَشِّرِ الْمُخْبِتِينَ﴾: he said, "The ones at peace (al-muṭmaʾinīn)."

Al-Shawkani, Fath al-Qadir (commentary on 22:30–35), part 2 of 2:

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *Dhamm al-Ghadab* (The Condemnation of Anger), Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* (The Branches of Faith) transmitted from ʿAmr ibn Awis, who said: "The *mukhbitun* (the humble, the lowly-hearted) in the verse are those who do not wrong people, and when they are wronged, they do not retaliate."

The place of ﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ (dhalika) is in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "the matter is thus," or as the subject of an omitted predicate. It may also be in the accusative, governed by an omitted verb, meaning "do that." What is referred to is the rites of the Hajj mentioned earlier. This word and its like (hadha and similar) are used to separate two statements or the two ends of a single statement. ﴿الحُرُماتُ﴾ (al-hurumat, "the sacred things") is the plural of ḥurmah (inviolable sanctity).

Al-Zajjaj said: the ḥurmah (inviolability) is that which must be upheld and whose neglect is forbidden. In this verse it is what has been prohibited and what one is barred from committing.

The apparent meaning of the verse is the generality of every sacred thing in the Hajj and elsewhere, as the wording indicates, even if the occasion of revelation was specific. Glorifying them (taʿẓīm) is abstaining from involvement with them. ﴿فَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لَهُ﴾ means: glorifying them is better for him with his Lord, that is, in the Hereafter, than being careless about any of them.

It has been said that the comparative form here (khayr, "better") is not meant in its literal sense. Rather, the meaning is that this glorification is a good from which one benefits, so it is a promise of good.

﴿وَأُحِلَّتْ لَكُمُ الأَنْعَامُ﴾: these are camels, cattle and sheep. ﴿إِلَّا مَا يُتْلَى عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ means: except what is recited to you in the Noble Book of the prohibited things, namely carrion and what is mentioned with it in Surat al-Ma'ida. It has been said that this refers to the statement ﴿إِلَّا مَا يُتْلَى عَلَيْكُمْ غَيْرَ مُحِلِّي الصَّيْدِ وَأَنْتُمْ حُرُمٌ﴾ (the exception being what is recited to you, not permitting game while you are in the state of iḥram).

﴿فَاجْتَنِبُوا الرِّجْسَ مِنَ الأَوْثَانِ﴾: the rijs is filth, and the wathan is an idol statue. Its root is from wathana al-shay', meaning he settled in its place. The cross was called a wathan because it is set up and fixed in its place and does not move from it. The intended meaning is avoiding the worship of idols. He called them rijs because they are the cause of rijs, which is punishment.

It has been said that Allah, glory be to Him, made them rijs by judgment. Rijs means najas (impurity). Impurity is not an inherent attribute of idols but a legal attribute, so it is removed only by faith, just as physical impurity is removed only by water.

Al-Zajjaj said: the "min" here (in min al-awthan) is for specifying a genus out of genera, meaning: avoid the filth which is idolatry. ﴿وَاجْتَنِبُوا قَوْلَ الزُّورِ﴾ (and avoid the word of falsehood) means the falsehood. It is called zūr because it inclines away from the truth. From the same root is His statement ﴿تَزَاوَرُ عَنْ كَهْفِهِمْ﴾ (it [the sun] inclines away from their cave), and the saying "a city zawrāʾ," meaning inclined. The intended meaning here is false speech in general, and the gravest of it is associating partners with Allah in any wording whatsoever.

Al-Zajjaj also said: the intended meaning of "word of falsehood" here is their declaring some of the livestock lawful and some unlawful, and their saying "this is lawful and this is unlawful." It has been said that it refers to false testimony.

The meaning is: give them glad tidings, O Muhammad, of the abundant reward and great gifts that Allah has prepared for them.

It has been said that the mukhbitīn are those who do not wrong others, and when others wrong them they do not seek retribution.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, described these mukhbitīn with His statement ﴿الَّذِينَ إِذَا ذُكِرَ اللَّهُ وَجِلَتْ قُلُوبُهُمْ﴾ (those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned), meaning they fear and beware of disobeying Him. The occurrence of trembling in them at the mention of Him, glory be to Him, is evidence of the perfection of their certainty and the strength of their faith. He described them with patience ﴿عَلَى مَا أَصَابَهُمْ﴾ (over what befalls them) of afflictions and trials in obedience to Allah. Then He described them with establishing the prayer, meaning performing it at its times in the most complete manner.

The majority read ﴿وَالْمُقِيمِي الصَّلَاةِ﴾ (wal-muqīmī al-ṣalāh) with a kasra, as is apparent. Abu ʿAmr read it with a fatḥa, as if the nūn were still retained (wal-muqīmīna). Sibawayh cited as evidence for that the verse of the poet:

"The guardian of the honour of the tribe..." (the whole line), with the accusative on ʿawrata (ʿawrah, honour/vulnerable point).

It has been said that Abu ʿAmr did not read with this reading. Ibn Muhaysin read wal-muqīmīna with the nūn retained according to the original form, and this reading is narrated from Ibn Masʿūd. Then He described them, glory be to Him, with His statement ﴿وَمِمَّا رَزَقْنَاهُمْ يُنْفِقُونَ﴾ (and from what We have provided them they spend), meaning they give charity from it, spending it in the paths of righteousness and placing it in the places of good. A similar verse is His statement, glory be to Him: ﴿إِنَّمَا الْمُؤْمِنُونَ الَّذِينَ إِذَا ذُكِرَ اللَّهُ وَجِلَتْ قُلُوبُهُمْ وَإِذَا تُلِيَتْ عَلَيْهِمْ آيَاتُهُ زَادَتْهُمْ إِيمَانًا وَعَلَى رَبِّهِمْ يَتَوَكَّلُونَ﴾ (The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, and when His verses are recited to them they increase them in faith, and upon their Lord they rely).

Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding His statement ﴿حُرُمَاتِ اللَّهِ﴾ (the sacred things of Allah): he said, "The sacred things are Makkah, the Hajj and the ʿUmrah, and everything Allah has forbidden of His disobediences, all of them."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His statement ﴿فَاجْتَنِبُوا الرِّجْسَ مِنَ الْأَوْثَانِ﴾: he said, "Avoid obeying Satan in the worship of idols." ﴿وَاجْتَنِبُوا قَوْلَ الزُّورِ﴾: he means slandering Allah and denying Him.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ayman ibn Khuraym, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood up delivering a sermon and said: "O people, false testimony has been made equal to associating partners with Allah," three times. Then he recited ﴿فَاجْتَنِبُوا الرِّجْسَ مِنَ الْأَوْثَانِ وَاجْتَنِبُوا قَوْلَ الزُّورِ﴾.

Ahmad said: it is gharīb (a strange narration); we know it only from the narration of Sufyan ibn Zayd. It has been differently reported from him in narrating this hadith, and we do not know of Ayman ibn Khuraym having heard from the Prophet (ﷺ).

It was also narrated by Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab, from the hadith of Khuraym.

It is firmly established in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs and others, from the hadith of Abu Bakra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Shall I not inform you of the greatest of the major sins?" three times. We said, "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said, "Associating partners with Allah, and disobedience to parents." He had been reclining, so he sat up and said, "Beware, and the word of falsehood. Beware, and false testimony." He kept repeating it until we said, "I wish he would stop."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His statement ﴿حُنَفَاءَ لِلَّهِ غَيْرَ مُشْرِكِينَ بِهِ﴾: he said, "Pilgrims to Allah, not associating anything with Him." This is because the people of jāhiliyyah used to make the pilgrimage while associating partners, but when Allah made Islam manifest, Allah said to the Muslims: "Make the pilgrimage now, not associating anything with Allah."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His statement ﴿وَمَنْ يُعَظِّمْ شَعَائِرَ اللَّهِ﴾: he said, "The budn (sacrificial camels)."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿وَمَنْ يُعَظِّمْ شَعَائِرَ اللَّهِ﴾: he said, "Choosing the fattest, the finest, and the most magnificent." And regarding His statement ﴿لَكُمْ فِيهَا مَنَافِعُ إِلَى أَجَلٍ مُسَمًّى﴾: he said, "Until they are named budn."

These same narrators also narrated similarly from Mujahid, and in it he said: "﴿لَكُمْ فِيهَا مَنَافِعُ إِلَى أَجَلٍ مُسَمًّى﴾: in their backs, their milk, their wool, their hair and their fleece, until they are named hady (sacrificial offering). When they are named hady, the benefits go away. Then ﴿مَحِلُّهَا﴾ (their place) — he says: when they are named — ﴿إِلَى الْبَيْتِ الْعَتِيقِ﴾."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʿIkrima, who said: "When it enters the Sacred Precinct, it has reached its place."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His statement ﴿وَلِكُلِّ أُمَّةٍ جَعَلْنَا مَنْسَكًا﴾: he said, "A festival."

Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding the verse: he said, "The shedding of blood."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from ʿIkrima, who said: "Slaughter."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam regarding the verse, who said: "Makkah. Allah has not appointed any community a mansak other than it."

Hadiths about the sacrifice (udhiyya) have been reported, but this is not the place to mention them.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding His statement ﴿وَبَشِّرِ الْمُخْبِتِينَ﴾: he said, "The ones at peace (al-muṭmaʾinīn)."

Al-Shawkani, Fath al-Qadir (commentary on 22:30–35), part 2 of 2:

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *Dhamm al-Ghadab* (The Condemnation of Anger), Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* (The Branches of Faith) transmitted from ʿAmr ibn Awis, who said: "The *mukhbitun* (the humble, the lowly-hearted) in the verse are those who do not wrong people, and when they are wronged, they do not retaliate."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 22, verses 36–37:

Ibn Abi Ishaq read *wal-budna* (وَالبُدُنَ) with a *damma* on the *ba'* and the *dal*, while the rest read it with a *sukun* on the *dal*. Both are dialectal forms (*lughatan*). This noun is specific to camels (*al-ibil*), and it was called *badana* because the animal grows fat (*tabdunu*), and *al-bada'na* means fatness.

Abu Hanifa and Malik said that it applies to animals other than camels. The first view is preferable, because of the descriptions that follow, which clearly apply to camels, and because the lexicon books indicate that this term is restricted to camels.

Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir: "They differed over whether it is correct to apply *badana* to the cow, in two views. The more sound of them is that it is applied to both by the Shari'a, as is established in the hadith." ﴿We have made them for you﴾, which was explained shortly before, ﴿for you there is good in them﴾, meaning religious and worldly benefits, as was mentioned before. ﴿So mention the name of Allah over them﴾, meaning over their kind. The meaning of *sawaff* (صَوَافَّ) is that they stand, their legs having been arranged, because they are slaughtered standing and tied up. The origin of this description is in horses: one says *safana al-faras* (صَفَنَ الفَرَسُ), so he is *safin* (صَافِنٌ), when he stands on three legs and bends the fourth.

Al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Mujahid, Zayd ibn Aslam and Abu Musa al-Ash'ari read *sawafi* (صَوَافِي), meaning pure for Allah, that you do not associate anyone with Him in the naming over their slaughter. The singular of *sawaff* is *saffa* (صَافَّةٌ), and this is the reading of the majority.

The singular of *sawafi* is *safiya* (صَافِيَةٌ). Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Umar, Ibn Abbas, Abu Ja'far and Muhammad ibn Ali read *sawafin* (صَوَافِنَ) with a *nun*, the plural of *safina* (صَافِنَةٌ). The *safina* is the one that has raised one of its forelegs while tied, so that it does not tremble. From this is the words of the Exalted: ﴿the well-bred steeds standing on three legs﴾ [Sad: 31]. From this is the saying of Amr ibn Kulthum:

"We left the horses sitting upon it, their bridles hung, standing on *sufun*."

Another said:

"He became accustomed to *sufun*, so that he always seems,
of those who stand on three legs, a lame one."

﴿Then when their sides fall﴾: *al-wujub* means falling, that is, they fall after being slaughtered, which happens when their soul departs. ﴿Then eat from them﴾. The majority held that this command is for recommendation (*nadb*). ﴿And feed the contented and the beggar﴾. This command is said to be for recommendation, like the first, and this was the view of Mujahid, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Surayj. Al-Shafi'i and a group said it is obligatory.

It is disputed who the *qani'* (القَانِعَ) is. It was said he is the one who asks. One says *qana'a al-rajul* (قَنَعَ الرَّجُلُ), with a *fatha* on the *nun*, *yaqna'u* (يَقْنِعُ) with a *kasra*, when he asks. From this is the saying of al-Shammakh:

"A man's wealth, which sets him right and makes him rich,
is more chaste than begging (*al-qunu'*)."

That is, asking. It was also said: he is the one who abstains from asking and is content with a sufficiency; al-Khalil mentioned this meaning.

Ibn al-Sikkit said: some Arabs use *al-qunu'* to mean *al-qana'a*, which is contentment, abstinence and leaving off asking.

Zayd ibn Aslam, his son, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Hasan held the first view, and it was narrated from Ibn Abbas. Ikrima and Qatada held the second.

As for *al-mu'tarr* (المُعْتَرَّ), Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, Mujahid, Ibrahim, al-Kalbi and al-Hasan said that it is the one who presents himself without asking. It was also said: he is the one who visits you and asks you.

Malik said: the best of what I have heard is that the *qani'* is the poor person and the *mu'tarr* is the visitor.

It was narrated from Ibn Abbas that both are the one who does not ask, but the *qani'* is the one who is content with what he has and does not ask, and the *mu'tarr* is the one who presents himself to you and does not ask you.

Al-Hasan read *al-mu'tari* (المُعْتَرِي), and its meaning is the same as *al-mu'tarr*. From this is the saying of Zuhayr:

"For their wealthy ones is the provision of whoever comes to them,
and among the poor is generosity and giving."

One says *i'tarrahu*, *i'taraahu*, *arrahu* and *arrahu* when he presents himself for what is with him or seeks it. This was mentioned by al-Nahhas.

﴿Thus We have subjected them to you﴾, meaning like that wondrous subjugation We have subjected them to you, so they submit to you to bring them to the places of slaughter, and you slaughter them and benefit from them, after they were subjected to you for carrying loads, riding on their backs, milking them and the like. ﴿So that you may give thanks﴾ for this blessing with which Allah has favoured you.

﴿Their flesh does not reach Allah, nor their blood﴾, meaning it does not ascend to Him, does not attain His pleasure, and does not come to acceptance with Him: neither the flesh of these camels that you give in charity, nor their blood that flows at their slaughter, insofar as they are flesh and blood. Rather, ﴿it is your piety that reaches Him﴾, meaning your hearts' taqwa reaches Him, your sincerity toward Him and your intention in this to seek His face. This is what Allah accepts and rewards.

It was said: the intended meaning is the owners of the flesh and blood, meaning that those who sacrifice and draw near to their Lord with flesh and blood are not pleased, but rather with piety.

Al-Zajjaj said: Allah has informed that what reaches Him is their piety and obedience in what He commands. The real meaning of this statement returns to acceptance, because what a person accepts is said to have been attained and reached. So Allah addressed the creatures in their customary manner of address.

﴿Thus He has subjected them to you﴾: this is repeated for reminder. The meaning of ﴿that you may glorify Allah for having guided you﴾ is the saying of the slaughterer, "Allah is greatest" at the slaughter. The first verse mentioned the command to mention the name of Allah over them, and here it mentions the glorification (*takbir*), to indicate the legitimacy of combining the naming and the glorification.

It was said: the intended meaning of *takbir* is describing Him, glorified be He, with what indicates greatness. The meaning of ﴿for having guided you﴾ is for having directed you to knowledge of how to draw near to Him through them. *Ma* here is either a verbal noun (*masdariyya*) or a relative pronoun (*mawsula*).

﴿And give good tidings to the good-doers﴾. It was said that they are the sincere, and it was said: the monotheists. The apparent meaning is that the intended ones are everyone from whom good proceeds such that the name "good-doer" (*muhsin*) can rightly be applied to him.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abdullah ibn Umar that he said: "We know *al-budn* only as camels and cows."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said: "*Al-budn* are those with a belly (*dhat al-jawf*)."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid that he said: "*Al-budn* are only camels." They also narrated similarly from al-Hakam, and narrated from Ata' something like what Ibn Umar said.

Ibn Abi Shayba narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan something similar, also (p. 966).

Ibn Abi Shayba and Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ya'qub al-Rabahi, from his father, that he said: "A man bequeathed a *badana*, so I came to Ibn Abbas and said to him: 'A man has appointed me as executor and bequeathed a *badana*; would a cow suffice for me?' He said: 'Yes.' Then he said: 'From which tribe is your companion?' I said: 'From Banu Rabah.' He said: 'When did Banu Rabah acquire cows in addition to camels? Your companion is mistaken. Cows belong only to Asad and Abd al-Qays.'"

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *al-Adahi*, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan, narrated from Abu Zibyan, who said: "I asked Ibn Abbas about His saying: ﴿So mention the name of Allah over them standing (*sawaff*)﴾. He said: 'When you want to slaughter the *badana*, stand it on three tied legs, then say: "In the name of Allah, Allah is greatest."'"

Al-Firyabi, Abu Ubayd, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through several chains from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying *sawaff*, that he said: "Standing and tied." In the two *Sahihs* and others, it is narrated from him that he saw a man who had made his *badana* kneel while slaughtering it, and he said: "Let it stand, tied, the Sunna of Muhammad (ﷺ, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family)."

Abu Ubayda, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Maymun ibn Mihran that he said: "In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, *sawafin* means standing."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, concerning ﴿then when they fall﴾, that he said: "They fell on their sides."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said: "They were slaughtered."

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him that he said: "*Al-qani'* is the one who is abstinent, and *al-mu'tarr* is the one who asks."

Ibn Abi Shayba narrated from Ibn Umar that he said: "*Al-qani'* is the one who is content with what you give him."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "*Al-qani'* is the one who is content with what he has been given, and *al-mu'tarr* is the one who comes across (you)."

He also narrated from him that he said: "*Al-qani'* is the one who sits in his house."

Abd ibn Humayd and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from him that he was asked about this verse, and he said: "As for *al-qani'*, he is the one who is content with what you send to him in his house, and *al-mu'tarr* is the one who visits you."

Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from him that he said: "*Al-qani'* is the one who asks, and *al-mu'tarr* is the one who presents himself and does not ask."

Various differing views have been narrated from the Successors (*tabi'un*) concerning the interpretation of this verse, and the reference is to the linguistic meaning, especially given the disagreement among the Companions and those after them in interpreting it.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "When the polytheists slaughtered, they faced the Ka'ba with the blood and sprinkled it toward the Ka'ba. The Muslims wanted to do the same, so Allah revealed: ﴿Their flesh does not reach Allah, nor their blood﴾." Ibn Abi Hatim narrated something similar from Ibn Jurayj.

It was said: the intended meaning of *takbir* is describing Him, glorified be He, with what indicates greatness. The meaning of ﴿for having guided you﴾ is for having directed you to knowledge of how to draw near to Him through them. *Ma* here is either a verbal noun (*masdariyya*) or a relative pronoun (*mawsula*).

﴿And give good tidings to the good-doers﴾. It was said that they are the sincere, and it was said: the monotheists. The apparent meaning is that the intended ones are everyone from whom good proceeds such that the name "good-doer" (*muhsin*) can rightly be applied to him.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abdullah ibn Umar that he said: "We know *al-budn* only as camels and cows."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said: "*Al-budn* are those with a belly (*dhat al-jawf*)."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid that he said: "*Al-budn* are only camels." They also narrated similarly from al-Hakam, and narrated from Ata' something like what Ibn Umar said.

Ibn Abi Shayba narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan something similar, also (p. 966).

Ibn Abi Shayba and Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ya'qub al-Rabahi, from his father, that he said: "A man bequeathed a *badana*, so I came to Ibn Abbas and said to him: 'A man has appointed me as executor and bequeathed a *badana*; would a cow suffice for me?' He said: 'Yes.' Then he said: 'From which tribe is your companion?' I said: 'From Banu Rabah.' He said: 'When did Banu Rabah acquire cows in addition to camels? Your companion is mistaken. Cows belong only to Asad and Abd al-Qays.'"

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *al-Adahi*, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan, narrated from Abu Zibyan, who said: "I asked Ibn Abbas about His saying: ﴿So mention the name of Allah over them standing (*sawaff*)﴾. He said: 'When you want to slaughter the *badana*, stand it on three tied legs, then say: "In the name of Allah, Allah is greatest."'"

Al-Firyabi, Abu Ubayd, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through several chains from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying *sawaff*, that he said: "Standing and tied." In the two *Sahihs* and others, it is narrated from him that he saw a man who had made his *badana* kneel while slaughtering it, and he said: "Let it stand, tied, the Sunna of Muhammad (ﷺ, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family)."

Abu Ubayda, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Maymun ibn Mihran that he said: "In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, *sawafin* means standing."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, concerning ﴿then when they fall﴾, that he said: "They fell on their sides."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said: "They were slaughtered."

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him that he said: "*Al-qani'* is the one who is abstinent, and *al-mu'tarr* is the one who asks."

Ibn Abi Shayba narrated from Ibn Umar that he said: "*Al-qani'* is the one who is content with what you give him."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "*Al-qani'* is the one who is content with what he has been given, and *al-mu'tarr* is the one who comes across (you)."

He also narrated from him that he said: "*Al-qani'* is the one who sits in his house."

Abd ibn Humayd and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from him that he was asked about this verse, and he said: "As for *al-qani'*, he is the one who is content with what you send to him in his house, and *al-mu'tarr* is the one who visits you."

Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from him that he said: "*Al-qani'* is the one who asks, and *al-mu'tarr* is the one who presents himself and does not ask."

Various differing views have been narrated from the Successors (*tabi'un*) concerning the interpretation of this verse, and the reference is to the linguistic meaning, especially given the disagreement among the Companions and those after them in interpreting it.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "When the polytheists slaughtered, they faced the Ka'ba with the blood and sprinkled it toward the Ka'ba. The Muslims wanted to do the same, so Allah revealed: ﴿Their flesh does not reach Allah, nor their blood﴾." Ibn Abi Hatim narrated something similar from Ibn Jurayj.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 22, verses 38–41:

Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read ﴿yadfa'u﴾ (يَدْفَعُ), and the rest read ﴿yudafi'u﴾ (يُدافِعُ). The form of the verb here (ṣīghat al-mufā'alah, the "mufa'alah" pattern) is stripped of its original meaning, which is that the action occurs from both sides, as the other reading indicates.

This form is often used without its original meaning, as in ʿāqabtu al-liṣṣ (I punished the thief) and similar examples, and we have already discussed its verification. It was said that the use of this form here is for emphasis (al-mubālaghah). It was also said that it indicates the repetition of the act.

The meaning is: He defends the believers against the calamities (ghawā'il) of the polytheists. It was said: He exalts their proof. It was said: He grants them success. The sentence is a fresh sentence (mustaʼnafah) explaining this distinction that the believers obtain from the Lord of the worlds, and that He is the one who undertakes their defence. The sentence ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love every treacherous ungrateful one﴾ confirms the content of the first sentence, for defence by Allah on behalf of His believing servants indicates most completely that they are hated by Allah and are not beloved to Him.

Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever mentions other than the name of Allah and draws near to idols through his sacrifice is a treacherous ungrateful one (khawwān kafūr). The use of the two intensive forms (ṣīghatay al-mubālaghah) is to indicate that they are actually like this, not to exclude one who betrays other than their betrayal, or disbelieves other than their disbelief.

﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged.﴾ The verb ﴿udhina﴾ (أُذِنَ) is read in the active and in the passive voice, and likewise ﴿yuqātalūna﴾ (يُقاتَلُونَ) is read in the active and in the passive voice. On both readings, the permission from Allah, glorified is He, to His believing servants is that when they are fit for fighting, or when the polytheists fight them, they may fight them.

The exegetes said: The polytheists of Makkah used to harm the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with their tongues and hands, and they would complain of that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he would say to them: "Be patient, for I have not been commanded to fight," until he emigrated (hijrah). Then Allah, glorified is He, revealed this verse at Madinah, and it is the first verse revealed concerning fighting.

This verse also confirms the content of His saying ﴿Indeed Allah defends﴾. The permission for them to fight is part of Allah's defence on their behalf. The bā' in ﴿bi-annahum ẓulimū﴾ (بِأنَّهم ظُلِمُوا) is causal (lil-sababiyyah), meaning: because they were wronged, by what was inflicted upon them by the polytheists of abuse, beating and expulsion. Then Allah, glorified is He, promised them victory over the polytheists, saying: ﴿And indeed Allah is competent to give them victory﴾. This also contains emphasis on the defence mentioned earlier.

Then He described these believers with His saying: ﴿Those who have been expelled from their homes without right﴾. It may be a substitute (badal) for ﴿those who are fought against﴾, or in the accusative place (maḥall naṣb) by way of praise, or in the nominative place (maḥall raf') by supposing an implied subject (bi-iḍmār mubtada'). The word "homes" (diyār) is intended to mean Makkah.

﴿Except that they say: Our Lord is Allah.﴾ Sibawayh said: This is a disjunctive exception (istithnā' munqaṭi'): meaning, "but because of their saying: Our Lord is Allah." That is: they were expelled without a right that would require their expulsion, but because of their saying: Our Lord is Allah.

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: It is a connected exception (istithnā' muttaṣil), and the estimate is: "Those who were expelled from their homes without any right, except that they say: Our Lord is Allah." This is like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And you do not resent us except that we believed﴾, and like the saying of al-Nabighah:

"There is no fault in them, except that their swords, from the clashing of the battalions, have notches (fulūl)."

﴿And had Allah not repelled some people by means of others...﴾ Nafi' read ﴿wa-lawlā difā'u﴾ (وَلَوْلا دِفاعُ), and the rest read ﴿wa-lawlā daf'u﴾ (وَلَوْلا دَفْعُ). The meaning: had it not been for what Allah prescribed for the prophets and believers of fighting against enemies, the people of polytheism would have prevailed, and the places of worship would have vanished from the earth. The meaning of "would have been demolished" (lahuddimat) is "would have been ruined" by the domination of the people of polytheism over the people of the religions (milal).

So the ṣawāmi' (صَوامِعُ) are the hermitages of the monks. It was said: the hermitages of the Sabians. The biya' (بِيَعُ) is the plural of biya'ah, which is the church of the Christians. The ṣalawāt (صَلَوَاتُ) are the synagogues of the Jews, and its name in Hebrew is ṣalūtha with the letter thā' (ث), then it was Arabized. The masājid (مَساجِدُ) are the mosques of the Muslims.

It was said: The meaning is: had it not been for this defence, the churches would have been demolished in the time of Musa (Moses), and the hermitages and churches in the time of 'Isa (Jesus), and the mosques in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is the most correct of what has been said concerning the interpretation of the verse. It was said: The meaning is: had it not been for Allah's repelling the oppression of oppressors through the justice of rulers. It was said: Had it not been for Allah's repelling punishment through the supplication of the righteous. It was said: other than that.

The ṣawāmi' is the plural of ṣawma'ah, which is a tall building. It is said ṣama'a al-tharīdah (صَمَعَ الثَّرِيدَةَ), meaning when he raised its head. And "rajul aṣma' al-qalb" means one sharp of intelligence. The aṣma' among men is one with a keen speech. It was said: one with small ears. Then the term was used for the places from which the call to prayer (adhān) is made in Islam.

Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned nine readings for ﴿ṣalawāt﴾ (صَلَواتٌ). The reason for placing the places of worship of the people of the religions before the place of worship of the Muslims is that they are older in construction and earlier in existence.

The apparent meaning of the demolition mentioned is its literal meaning, as Al-Zajjaj and others mentioned. It was said: What is meant is the figurative meaning, which is their being rendered idle from worship. It was read ﴿lahuddimat﴾ with emphasis (tashdīd). The accusative of ﴿kathīran﴾ (كَثِيرًا) in His saying ﴿in which the name of Allah is mentioned much﴾ is that it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (maṣdar maḥdhūf), meaning: a great mention, or a long time. The clause is an adjective of the mosques. It was said: it is an adjective of all that has been mentioned.

﴿And Allah will surely support those who support Him.﴾ The lām (لَ) is the answer to an omitted oath, meaning: By Allah, Allah will surely support whoever supports Him. What is meant by "whoever supports Allah" is whoever supports His religion and His allies. "Al-qawiyy" is the one capable of something. "Al-'azīz" is the majestic, noble. Al-Zajjaj said this. It was said: the one who is invincible, who cannot be assailed, repelled, or prevented.

The relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl) in His saying ﴿Those who, if We establish them in the land﴾ is in the accusative place as an adjective of "whoever" (man) in His saying "whoever supports Him." Al-Zajjaj said this. Others said it is in the genitive place as an adjective of His saying "those who are fought against."

It was said: What is meant by them are the emigrants (muhājirūn), the helpers (anṣār), and those who follow them in goodness. It was said: the people of the five prayers. It was said: the rulers of justice. It was said: other than that. In it is the obligation of enjoining good and forbidding evil upon whoever Allah has established in the land and empowered to carry this out.

The interpretation of the verse has already been given. The meaning of ﴿And to Allah belongs the outcome of affairs﴾ is that their return is to His judgment and His management, not to other than Him.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it ḥasan), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who graded it ṣaḥīḥ), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) was expelled from Makkah, Abu Bakr said: 'They have expelled their Prophet! ﴿Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:156]. The people will surely perish.' Then this was revealed: ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged﴾, the verse."

Ibn 'Abbas said: It is the first verse revealed concerning fighting. al-Tirmidhi said: ḥasan. It has been transmitted by more than one from al-Thawri, and in it there is no mention of Ibn 'Abbas. End.

Something similar has been reported from a group of the Successors (tabi'un).

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: ﴿Those who have been expelled from their homes﴾, meaning from Makkah to Madinah, without right, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ) and his companions.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, who said: This verse was revealed concerning us: ﴿those who have been expelled from their homes without right﴾, and the verse after it, "We have been expelled from our homes without right" ... then: ﴿if We establish them in the land, they establish prayer, give zakat, enjoin good and forbid evil﴾. So it is for me and my companions.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: This verse was only revealed concerning the Companions of Muhammad: ﴿And had Allah not repelled some people...﴾, the verse. He said: Had it not been for Allah's repelling by means of the Companions of Muhammad the followers, the hermitages would have been demolished.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿the hermitages would have been demolished﴾, the verse, that he said: The ṣawāmi' are those in which the monks are; the biya' are the mosques of the Jews; the ṣalawāt are the churches of the Christians; and the masājid are the mosques of the Muslims.

Both of them also transmitted from him, who said: The biya' are the churches of the Christians, and the ṣalawāt are the synagogues of the Jews.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Zayd ibn Aslam concerning His saying ﴿those who, if We establish them in the land﴾, that he said: The land of Madinah. ﴿They establish prayer﴾: he said: the obligatory prayer. ﴿And give zakat﴾: he said: the obligatory zakat. ﴿And enjoin good﴾: he said: "There is no god but Allah." ﴿And forbid evil﴾: he said: from polytheism with Allah. ﴿And to Allah belongs the outcome of affairs﴾: he said: and with Allah is the reward of what they did.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 22, verses 38–41:

Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read ﴿yadfa'u﴾ (يَدْفَعُ), and the rest read ﴿yudafi'u﴾ (يُدافِعُ). The form of the verb here (ṣīghat al-mufā'alah, the "mufa'alah" pattern) is stripped of its original meaning, which is that the action occurs from both sides, as the other reading indicates.

This form is often used without its original meaning, as in ʿāqabtu al-liṣṣ (I punished the thief) and similar examples, and we have already discussed its verification. It was said that the use of this form here is for emphasis (al-mubālaghah). It was also said that it indicates the repetition of the act.

The meaning is: He defends the believers against the calamities (ghawā'il) of the polytheists. It was said: He exalts their proof. It was said: He grants them success. The sentence is a fresh sentence (mustaʼnafah) explaining this distinction that the believers obtain from the Lord of the worlds, and that He is the one who undertakes their defence. The sentence ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love every treacherous ungrateful one﴾ confirms the content of the first sentence, for defence by Allah on behalf of His believing servants indicates most completely that they are hated by Allah and are not beloved to Him.

Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever mentions other than the name of Allah and draws near to idols through his sacrifice is a treacherous ungrateful one (khawwān kafūr). The use of the two intensive forms (ṣīghatay al-mubālaghah) is to indicate that they are actually like this, not to exclude one who betrays other than their betrayal, or disbelieves other than their disbelief.

﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged.﴾ The verb ﴿udhina﴾ (أُذِنَ) is read in the active and in the passive voice, and likewise ﴿yuqātalūna﴾ (يُقاتَلُونَ) is read in the active and in the passive voice. On both readings, the permission from Allah, glorified is He, to His believing servants is that when they are fit for fighting, or when the polytheists fight them, they may fight them.

The exegetes said: The polytheists of Makkah used to harm the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with their tongues and hands, and they would complain of that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he would say to them: "Be patient, for I have not been commanded to fight," until he emigrated (hijrah). Then Allah, glorified is He, revealed this verse at Madinah, and it is the first verse revealed concerning fighting.

This verse also confirms the content of His saying ﴿Indeed Allah defends﴾. The permission for them to fight is part of Allah's defence on their behalf. The bā' in ﴿bi-annahum ẓulimū﴾ (بِأنَّهم ظُلِمُوا) is causal (lil-sababiyyah), meaning: because they were wronged, by what was inflicted upon them by the polytheists of abuse, beating and expulsion. Then Allah, glorified is He, promised them victory over the polytheists, saying: ﴿And indeed Allah is competent to give them victory﴾. This also contains emphasis on the defence mentioned earlier.

Then He described these believers with His saying: ﴿Those who have been expelled from their homes without right﴾. It may be a substitute (badal) for ﴿those who are fought against﴾, or in the accusative place (maḥall naṣb) by way of praise, or in the nominative place (maḥall raf') by supposing an implied subject (bi-iḍmār mubtada'). The word "homes" (diyār) is intended to mean Makkah.

﴿Except that they say: Our Lord is Allah.﴾ Sibawayh said: This is a disjunctive exception (istithnā' munqaṭi'): meaning, "but because of their saying: Our Lord is Allah." That is: they were expelled without a right that would require their expulsion, but because of their saying: Our Lord is Allah.

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: It is a connected exception (istithnā' muttaṣil), and the estimate is: "Those who were expelled from their homes without any right, except that they say: Our Lord is Allah." This is like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And you do not resent us except that we believed﴾, and like the saying of al-Nabighah:

"There is no fault in them, except that their swords, from the clashing of the battalions, have notches (fulūl)."

﴿And had Allah not repelled some people by means of others...﴾ Nafi' read ﴿wa-lawlā difā'u﴾ (وَلَوْلا دِفاعُ), and the rest read ﴿wa-lawlā daf'u﴾ (وَلَوْلا دَفْعُ). The meaning: had it not been for what Allah prescribed for the prophets and believers of fighting against enemies, the people of polytheism would have prevailed, and the places of worship would have vanished from the earth. The meaning of "would have been demolished" (lahuddimat) is "would have been ruined" by the domination of the people of polytheism over the people of the religions (milal).

So the ṣawāmi' (صَوامِعُ) are the hermitages of the monks. It was said: the hermitages of the Sabians. The biya' (بِيَعُ) is the plural of biya'ah, which is the church of the Christians. The ṣalawāt (صَلَوَاتُ) are the synagogues of the Jews, and its name in Hebrew is ṣalūtha with the letter thā' (ث), then it was Arabized. The masājid (مَساجِدُ) are the mosques of the Muslims.

It was said: The meaning is: had it not been for this defence, the churches would have been demolished in the time of Musa (Moses), and the hermitages and churches in the time of 'Isa (Jesus), and the mosques in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is the most correct of what has been said concerning the interpretation of the verse. It was said: The meaning is: had it not been for Allah's repelling the oppression of oppressors through the justice of rulers. It was said: Had it not been for Allah's repelling punishment through the supplication of the righteous. It was said: other than that.

The ṣawāmi' is the plural of ṣawma'ah, which is a tall building. It is said ṣama'a al-tharīdah (صَمَعَ الثَّرِيدَةَ), meaning when he raised its head. And "rajul aṣma' al-qalb" means one sharp of intelligence. The aṣma' among men is one with a keen speech. It was said: one with small ears. Then the term was used for the places from which the call to prayer (adhān) is made in Islam.

Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned nine readings for ﴿ṣalawāt﴾ (صَلَواتٌ). The reason for placing the places of worship of the people of the religions before the place of worship of the Muslims is that they are older in construction and earlier in existence.

The apparent meaning of the demolition mentioned is its literal meaning, as Al-Zajjaj and others mentioned. It was said: What is meant is the figurative meaning, which is their being rendered idle from worship. It was read ﴿lahuddimat﴾ with emphasis (tashdīd). The accusative of ﴿kathīran﴾ (كَثِيرًا) in His saying ﴿in which the name of Allah is mentioned much﴾ is that it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (maṣdar maḥdhūf), meaning: a great mention, or a long time. The clause is an adjective of the mosques. It was said: it is an adjective of all that has been mentioned.

﴿And Allah will surely support those who support Him.﴾ The lām (لَ) is the answer to an omitted oath, meaning: By Allah, Allah will surely support whoever supports Him. What is meant by "whoever supports Allah" is whoever supports His religion and His allies. "Al-qawiyy" is the one capable of something. "Al-'azīz" is the majestic, noble. Al-Zajjaj said this. It was said: the one who is invincible, who cannot be assailed, repelled, or prevented.

The relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl) in His saying ﴿Those who, if We establish them in the land﴾ is in the accusative place as an adjective of "whoever" (man) in His saying "whoever supports Him." Al-Zajjaj said this. Others said it is in the genitive place as an adjective of His saying "those who are fought against."

It was said: What is meant by them are the emigrants (muhājirūn), the helpers (anṣār), and those who follow them in goodness. It was said: the people of the five prayers. It was said: the rulers of justice. It was said: other than that. In it is the obligation of enjoining good and forbidding evil upon whoever Allah has established in the land and empowered to carry this out.

The interpretation of the verse has already been given. The meaning of ﴿And to Allah belongs the outcome of affairs﴾ is that their return is to His judgment and His management, not to other than Him.

Ibn 'Abbas said: It is the first verse revealed concerning fighting. al-Tirmidhi said: ḥasan. It has been transmitted by more than one from al-Thawri, and in it there is no mention of Ibn 'Abbas. End.

Something similar has been reported from a group of the Successors (tabi'un).

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 22, verses 42–51:

.

His saying: "And if they deny you..." This is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family) and a comfort to him, containing a promise to him that the deniers will be destroyed, just as Allah, glorified is He, destroyed the deniers of those who came before him.

In it is also guidance to him (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family) to be patient with his people and to follow the example of the prophets before him in that. The mention of these nations, what came from them and from their prophets, and how their end turned out, has already been made.

He changed the structure in His saying: ﴿And Musa was denied﴾, bringing the verb in the passive form, because the people of Musa did not deny him; rather, others among the Copts denied him. ﴿Then I gave the disbelievers respite﴾, meaning I delayed punishment from them and granted them a period. The "fa" indicates the sequence of the respite following the denial. (p-968) ﴿Then I seized them﴾, meaning I seized each group of the deniers with punishment after the period of respite had ended. ﴿So how was My rejection?﴾ This interrogative is for affirmation, meaning: consider how My disapproval of them was, and the change of the blessings they were in, and their destruction. "Nakir" is a noun derived from "munkar."

Al-Zajjaj said: meaning, "Then I seized them, and I rejected them with the utmost rejection." Al-Jawhari said: "Nakir" and "inkar" mean changing the disapproved thing.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned how He punished the people of the denying towns, saying: ﴿How many a town have We destroyed while it was wrongdoing﴾, meaning We destroyed its people. The discussion of this construction has already been made in Al 'Imran. It is also read as ("ahlaktuha," "I destroyed it"). The clause ﴿while it was wrongdoing﴾ is a circumstantial clause. The clause ﴿so it lies in ruins﴾ is coordinated with ("ahlaknaha," "We destroyed it"), not with ("zalima," "wrongdoing"), because the latter is a circumstantial clause, and the punishment does not occur during the state of wrongdoing. The attribution of wrongdoing to the town is meant as an attribution to its people. "Al-Khawa" means falling down, meaning: it has fallen upon its roofs (ʿurush), that is, upon its ceilings. This happened because its inhabitants were gone, until its walls collapsed on top of its ceilings. The interpretation of this verse has already been given in al-Baqara. ﴿And a well abandoned﴾ is coordinated with "town." The meaning: how many a town and how many of the people of an abandoned well? Thus said al-Zajjaj.

Al-Farra' said: it is coordinated with "its roofs," and "abandoned" means left behind.

It was also said: empty of its people due to their destruction. It was said: dried up. It was said: abandoned from buckets and ropes.

﴿And a lofty palace﴾: "mashid" is that which is high in its construction; thus said Qatada and al-Dahhak, and the saying of ʿAdi ibn Zayd supports it:

*He raised it with marble and coated it with plaster, so for birds in its heights there are nests.*

Will you not then reason?﴾ [As-Saffat: 137–138]. It was said that the seat of intellect is the brain, and there is no objection to that, for the heart is what prompts the perception of intellect, even if its seat is outside it.

Therefore He said: ﴿And Allah will not fail His promise﴾. Al-Farra' said: in this verse is a threat to them of punishment in this world and the Hereafter.

Al-Zajjaj mentioned another aspect, saying: I know that nothing escapes Allah, and that a day with Him and a thousand years in His power are one, and there is no difference between the occurrence of the punishment they are urging and its delay in terms of power, except that Allah has graciously granted respite. End.

The position of the clause ﴿And Allah will not fail His promise﴾ (p-969) is accusative as a circumstantial clause, meaning: and the state is that He does not fail His promise ever, and the promise has preceded, so it must come definitely. Or it is a parenthetical clause explaining what precedes it. According to the first, the clause ﴿And indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾ is a new sentence. According to the second, it is coordinated with the clause before it, presented to clarify their state in urging, and their address in that is by explaining the completeness of His forbearance, because a short period with Him is like a long period with them, as in His saying: ﴿They see it as distant, and We see it as near﴾ [Al-Ma'arij: 6–7]. Al-Farra' said: this is a threat to them of the prolongation of their punishment in the Hereafter, meaning: a day of the days of their punishment in the Hereafter is like a thousand years.

It was also said: the meaning is: a day of fear and hardship in the Hereafter is like a thousand years of the years of this world in which there is fear and hardship; likewise a day of bliss by analogy.

Ibn Kathir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read ("mimma ta'uddun," "of what you count") with the yaʾ (third person), and Abu ʿUbayd chose this reading because of His saying: ﴿and they ask you to hasten﴾. The rest read it with the taʾ (second person), addressed, and Abu Hatim chose it.

﴿And how many a town I gave respite while it was wrongdoing, then I seized it, and to Me is the return﴾. This is an announcement from Him, glorified is He, that He seized a people after giving them respite and delay.

It was said: the repetition of this, with its mention before, is for emphasis, and it is not a repetition in reality, because the first was given to explain the destruction, fitting His saying: ﴿So how was My rejection?﴾, and therefore it is joined with "fa" in place of that. The second was given to explain the respite, fitting His saying: ﴿And Allah will not fail His promise. And indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years﴾. It is as if it were said: how many a people of a town were like you, wrongdoers, whom I granted respite for a time, then I seized them with punishment, and all of them return to My judgment. So the clause ﴿and to Me is the return﴾ is a concluding statement to affirm what precedes it.

Then Allah, glorified is He, commanded him to tell the people that he is a warner to them before the Hour, clarifying to them what has been sent down to them. Whoever believes and does righteous deeds will succeed with forgiveness and generous provision, which is Paradise. As for whoever is contrary to that, he is in the Fire, and they are those who strive against the signs of Allah, seeking to frustrate them. It is said: ʿajazahu means he competed with him, because each of the two seeks to overcome the other; if one outpaces the other, it is said "a'jazahu" and "ʿajjazahu." This was said by al-Akhfash.

It was said: the meaning of "mu'ajizin" is: supposing and imagining that they could overcome Allah, glorified is He, and escape Him, so He would not punish them. This was said by al-Zajjaj. It was said: "opposing," said by al-Farra'.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatada, regarding His saying: ﴿so it lies in ruins upon its roofs﴾, he said: ruined, with no one in it. ﴿And an abandoned well﴾: its people abandoned it and left it. ﴿And a lofty palace﴾: he said: they built it and fortified it, then they perished and left it.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿And an abandoned well﴾, he said: the one that was left with no people.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him: ﴿And a lofty palace﴾, he said: it is the plastered one. ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Mujahid something similar. ʿAbd al-Razzaq and ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from ʿAta' something similar as well.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿And indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾, he said: of the six days in which Allah created the heavens and the earth.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʿIkrima, who said regarding the verse: it is the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, saying: this world is one Friday of the Fridays of the Hereafter, seven thousand years, of which six thousand have passed.

Ibn ʿAdi and al-Daylami narrated from Anas, marfu', something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding "mu'ajizin," he said: "muraghimin" (opposing). Ibn Jarir narrated from him that he said: "mushaqqin" (defying).

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 22, verses 42–51:

.

His saying: "And if they deny you..." This is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family) and a comfort to him, containing a promise to him that the deniers will be destroyed, just as Allah, glorified is He, destroyed the deniers of those who came before him.

In it is also guidance to him (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family) to be patient with his people and to follow the example of the prophets before him in that. The mention of these nations, what came from them and from their prophets, and how their end turned out, has already been made.

He changed the structure in His saying: ﴿And Musa was denied﴾, bringing the verb in the passive form, because the people of Musa did not deny him; rather, others among the Copts denied him. ﴿Then I gave the disbelievers respite﴾, meaning I delayed punishment from them and granted them a period. The "fa" indicates the sequence of the respite following the denial. (p-968) ﴿Then I seized them﴾, meaning I seized each group of the deniers with punishment after the period of respite had ended. ﴿So how was My rejection?﴾ This interrogative is for affirmation, meaning: consider how My disapproval of them was, and the change of the blessings they were in, and their destruction. "Nakir" is a noun derived from "munkar."

Al-Zajjaj said: meaning, "Then I seized them, and I rejected them with the utmost rejection." Al-Jawhari said: "Nakir" and "inkar" mean changing the disapproved thing.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned how He punished the people of the denying towns, saying: ﴿How many a town have We destroyed while it was wrongdoing﴾, meaning We destroyed its people. The discussion of this construction has already been made in Al 'Imran. It is also read as ("ahlaktuha," "I destroyed it"). The clause ﴿while it was wrongdoing﴾ is a circumstantial clause. The clause ﴿so it lies in ruins﴾ is coordinated with ("ahlaknaha," "We destroyed it"), not with ("zalima," "wrongdoing"), because the latter is a circumstantial clause, and the punishment does not occur during the state of wrongdoing. The attribution of wrongdoing to the town is meant as an attribution to its people. "Al-Khawa" means falling down, meaning: it has fallen upon its roofs (ʿurush), that is, upon its ceilings. This happened because its inhabitants were gone, until its walls collapsed on top of its ceilings. The interpretation of this verse has already been given in al-Baqara. ﴿And a well abandoned﴾ is coordinated with "town." The meaning: how many a town and how many of the people of an abandoned well? Thus said al-Zajjaj.

Al-Farra' said: it is coordinated with "its roofs," and "abandoned" means left behind.

It was also said: empty of its people due to their destruction. It was said: dried up. It was said: abandoned from buckets and ropes.

﴿And a lofty palace﴾: "mashid" is that which is high in its construction; thus said Qatada and al-Dahhak, and the saying of ʿAdi ibn Zayd supports it:

*He raised it with marble and coated it with plaster, so for birds in its heights there are nests.*

"Shadah" means he raised it. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, ʿAta', ʿIkrima, and Mujahid said: "mashid" means plastered, derived from "shid," which is plaster (gypsum), and from it is the saying of the rajiz:

*Do not think me, even if I am an ignorant man, like a snake of water between clay and plaster.*

It was also said: "mashid" means fortified; this was said by al-Kalbi.

Al-Jawhari said: "mashid" means built with shid, and "shid" with a kasra is everything with which you smear a wall, of plaster or flagstone; with a fatha it is the verbal noun. You say "shadah yashiduhu," meaning he plastered it. "Mushayyad" with a shadda means elongated.

Al-Kisa'i said: it is for the singular in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿in towers well-built﴾ [An-Nisa: 78]. The intended meaning: How many a lofty palace abandoned, like the abandoned well? The abandonment of the palace means that it is left without its people, or without its implements, or something similar.

Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir: It is said that this well and this palace are well known in Hadramawt. The palace overlooks the top of a mountain that cannot be reached by any means, and the well is at its foot, where the wind does not leave anything that falls into it without bringing it out. The people of the palace were kings of the settled lands, and the people of the well were kings of the desert.

Then he mentioned a long story, and said after that: As for the lofty palace, it was a palace built by Shaddad ibn ʿAd ibn Iram. It was not built on earth like it, according to what they mention and claim. Its condition is also like the condition of this well mentioned, in its desolation after intimacy, and its emptiness after prosperity, and no one can approach it within miles, because of what is heard in it of the howling of jinn and the strange sounds, after the bliss and pleasant life, the splendor of kingship, and the order of the people like a string of pearls. So they hastened and did not return. Thus Allah, glorified is He, mentioned them in this verse as an admonition and a lesson.

He said: It was also said: they are the ones whom Bukhtnasr destroyed, as has already been mentioned in Surat al-Anbiya' in His saying: ﴿How many a town have We shattered﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 11], so their well became abandoned and their palaces were ruined. End.

Then He, glorified is He, denounced the people of Makkah for not taking heed of these traces, saying: ﴿Have they not traveled through the earth﴾, urging them to travel so that they might see the places where those nations fell, and thus take heed. It is possible that they had traveled and did not take heed, which is why He denounced them, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed, you pass by them in the morning and at night. Will you not then reason?﴾ [As-Saffat: 137–138]. The meaning of ﴿so that they may have hearts by which they reason﴾ is that, because of what they witnessed of lessons, they would have hearts by which they reason about what they ought to reason about. He attributed reasoning to the hearts because they are the seat of intellect, just as ears are the seat of hearing. It was said that the seat of intellect is the brain, and there is no objection to that, for the heart is what prompts the perception of intellect, even if its seat is outside it.

The scholars of rational sciences have differed greatly about the seat of the intellect and its essence, and there is no need to lengthen by mentioning it. ﴿Or ears by which they hear﴾, meaning what they ought to hear of what their prophets recited to them of Allah's speech, and what the transmitters of reports conveyed to them of the reports of the destroyed nations. ﴿For indeed, it is not the eyes that go blind﴾. Al-Farra' said: the "ha'" is an expletive which may be said as ("fa-innahu"), and this is the reading of ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud. The meaning is one: the masculine form refers to the report, and the feminine refers to the eyes or the story, meaning: indeed the eyes do not go blind, or indeed the story does not blind the eyes, that is, the eyes of the sight. ﴿But it is the hearts within the breasts that go blind﴾, meaning the defect is not in their senses, but in their intellects, that is, their intellects do not perceive the places of truth and the locations of lesson.

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: His saying "which are in the breasts" is an emphasis which the Arabs add to speech, like His saying: ﴿ten complete﴾ [Al-Baqara: 196], ﴿they say with their mouths﴾ [Al 'Imran: 167], and ﴿flies with its two wings﴾ [Al-An'am: 38].
